a.etymology: Continues Latin ad ('to, toward, at'), with apocope of final -d before consonants (triggered syntactic gemination, raddoppiamento fonosintattico, preserved in univerbated compounds like accanto and allora) and retention of ad before vowels.

abbassare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *abbassiāre ('to lower, bring down'), parasynthetic verb formed from ad- ('to') + Late Latin bassus ('low, short').

abitare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin habitāre ('to dwell, inhabit, reside'), frequentative of habēre ('to have, hold').

accanto.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase a canto ('at the side, beside'), from a (< Latin ad) + canto ('edge, corner, side', from Late Latin canthus < Ancient Greek kanthós), with syntactic gemination of -c-.

accendere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin accendĕre ('to set on fire, kindle, light'), compound of ad- ('to') + *candĕre / candēre ('to glow white-hot, shine').

history.meaning: to kindle, light, set on fire
to light, turn on, switch on

accettare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin acceptāre ('to take, receive willingly'), frequentative verb built on accipĕre ('to receive, accept', from ad- + capĕre, 'to take').

acciaio.etymology: Continues Late Latin aciārium ('steely edge, steel'), derived from Latin acĭēs ('sharp edge, keen blade').

accogliente.etymology: Participial adjective from the present participle of accogliere (< Vulgar Latin *accolligĕre, 'to gather in, receive, welcome'), meaning 'welcoming, hospitable, cozy'.

accogliere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *accolligĕre ('to gather in, receive, welcome'), compound of ad- ('to') + Classical Latin colligĕre ('to gather, collect').

accomodarsi.etymology: Reflexive form of accomodare, learned adaptation of Classical Latin accommodāre ('to fit, adapt, make suitable', from ad- + commodus, 'convenient, comfortable'); in reflexive use 'to make oneself comfortable, take a seat'.

history.meaning: to make oneself comfortable, sit down

accordare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *accordāre (from cor, cordis, 'heart', meaning 'to bring into harmony'), re-associated in music with corda ('instrument string').

accordo.etymology: Deverbal noun from accordare (< Vulgar Latin *accordāre, from cor, cordis, 'heart'), later aligned in musical terminology with corda ('string').

aceto.etymology: Continues Latin acētum ('sour wine, vinegar'), substantivised neuter past participle linked to acēre ('to be sour').

acqua.etymology: Continues Latin aqua ('water'), with regular Tuscan gemination of the labiovelar stop before /w/ (/ˈakkwa/, spelled cq).

acustico.etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin acūsticus, from Ancient Greek ἀκουστικός (akoustikós, 'pertaining to hearing'), derived from ἀκούειν (akoúein, 'to hear').

addetta.etymology: Feminine noun and participial adjective from addetto, continuing Classical Latin addĭctus ('assigned, devoted, bound to'), past participle of addīcĕre ('to adjudge, assign, dedicate', from ad- + dīcĕre).

addolcire.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- (< Latin ad-) + dolce ('sweet', < Latin dulcis) + -ire, with regular syntactic gemination of -d-, meaning 'to sweeten, soften, mellow'.

adesso.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *ad ipsum (tempus) ('at this very moment'), or *ad id ipsum, attested early in northern Italian and Gallo-Romance before spreading into general Italian.

adorare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin adōrāre ('to speak to, pray to, worship, adore'), compound of ad- ('toward') + ōrāre ('to speak, pray', from ōs, ōris, 'mouth').

affacciarsi.etymology: Reflexive parasynthetic verb formed within Italian from a- (< Latin ad-) + faccia ('face', < Vulgar Latin *facia for Classical faciēs), literally 'to show one's face (at a window or threshold), look out'.

history.meaning: face -> to lean out, look out a window

affamato.etymology: Participial adjective from affamare ('to starve, make hungry'), parasynthetic verb formed from a- (< Latin ad-) + fame ('hunger', < Latin famēs, *famīna).

affare.etymology: Univerbation of the infinitival phrase (avere) a fare ('to have to do', paralleled by Old French afaire < a faire), substantivized in the 13th century as 'matter, business, deal, bargain'.

affatto.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase a fatto ('completely, in every respect'), from a (< Latin ad) + fatto (< Latin factum, 'deed, fact'); through frequent occurrence in negative clauses (non ... affatto), it also acquired a standalone negative sense ('not at all').

affidabile.etymology: Adjective derived from affidare ('to entrust, rely on', from Medieval/Vulgar Latin *affīdāre, built on fīdus / fīdēs, 'trust, faith') + the suffix -bile (< Latin -bĭlis).

affittare.etymology: Denominative verb from affitto (or Medieval Latin affictāre), built on ad- + Late/Medieval Latin fictus ('fixed [rent]', popular past participle of fīgĕre, 'to fix, fasten').

history.meaning: fixed rent / to lease for a fixed rent

affitto.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin affictus ('fixed rent or lease payment'), substantivized from ad- + fictus (popular past participle of Latin fīgĕre, 'to fix, establish' alongside классический fixus).

agganciare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Italian from a- (< Latin ad-) + gancio ('hook, clasp') + -are, with regular syntactic gemination of -g-.

agitarsi.etymology: Reflexive form of agitare ('to shake, stir, agitate'), learned continuation of Classical Latin agitāre (frequentative of agĕre, 'to drive, set in motion').

history.meaning: to drive -> to shake, stir up, agitate
to get agitated, move restlessly, worry

agitato.etymology: Participial adjective from agitare, continuing Classical Latin agitātus (past participle of agitāre, 'to toss, stir up, agitate').

agli.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of a ('to, at', < Latin ad) + the masculine plural definite article gli (< Old Italian li < Latin illī).

history.meaning: to the, at the (masculine plural before vowel/s+consonant/z)

ah.etymology: Primary expressive interjection of surprise, realization, relief, or regret, continuing Classical Latin ah / ā of natural vocal origin.

aha.etymology: Reduplicated expressive interjection of sudden realization, discovery, or satisfaction (ah + ah), attested across Romance and Germanic languages (cf. Latin ahaha).

ahi.etymology: Expressive interjection of sudden physical pain or distress, attested in Tuscan since the 13th century (Dante) and parallel to Old French ahi and Provençal ai.

ai.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of a ('to, at', < Latin ad) + the masculine plural definite article i (reduced from Old Italian li < Latin illī).

aiutare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin adiūtāre ('to help, assist'), frequentative of adiuvāre (from ad- + iuvāre, 'to help, aid'), with regular Tuscan palatal glide evolution of -di- to -i-.

al.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of a ('to, at', < Latin ad) + the masculine singular definite article il (via Old Italian a lo > al, from Latin ad illum).

alba.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(lūx) alba ('white morning light'), feminine of Classical Latin albus ('matt white').

albergo.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Gothic *haribairgo or Lombardic *haribergo ('military quarters, shelter, lodging', from Proto-Germanic *harjabergō: *harjaz 'army' + *bergō 'shelter, protection').

albero.etymology: Continues Latin arbŏr, arbŏrem ('tree'), with regular dissimilation of the first r to l (*albor).

alla.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of a ('to, at', < Latin ad) + the feminine singular definite article la (< Latin illam), with regular syntactic gemination of -l-.

alle.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of a ('to, at', < Latin ad) + the feminine plural definite article le (< Latin illās / illae), with regular syntactic gemination of -l-.

allentare.etymology: Continues Late/Vulgar Latin allentāre ('to slacken, slow down, loosen'), parasynthetic verb formed from ad- ('to') + Latin lentus ('pliable, slack, slow').

allo.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of a ('to, at', < Latin ad) + the masculine singular definite article lo (< Latin illum), with regular syntactic gemination of -l-.

history.meaning: to the, at the (masculine singular before vowel/s+consonant/z)

allora.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase all'ora ('at that hour, then'), continuing Latin ad illam hōram ('at that hour').

history.meaning: then, at that time; so, well then

almeno.etymology: Univerbation of the phrase al meno ('at the least'), from the articulated preposition al (< Latin ad illum) + meno ('less, least', < Latin mĭnus).

alone.etymology: Continues Late Latin halō, halōnis ('luminous ring around sun or moon'), from Greek ἅλως (hálōs, 'threshing floor; circular disc, halo').

alto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin altus ('high, tall, deep'), originally the old past participle of alĕre ('to nourish, make grow').

history.meaning: to nourish, rear -> grown high, tall, deep

altro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin alter, altĕrum ('the other of two'), which in Vulgar Latin generalized to replace alius ('another of many') for all senses of 'other'.

alzare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *altiāre ('to raise, lift up, make higher'), denominative verb derived from Classical Latin altus ('high').

amare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin amāre ('to love, hold dear, be fond of').

amico.etymology: Continues Latin amīcus ('friend'), built on the root of amāre ('to love').

anche.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *anque (probably a blend of Latin adhūc or ante with que / unquam, parallel to Old French ainc and Old Occitan anc), attested in Tuscan since the 12th–13th centuries.

ancora.etymology: Univerbation of Vulgar Latin (ad) hanc hōram ('to/at this very hour, still, yet'), parallel to French encore and Catalan encara.

andare.etymology: Suppletive verb combining two roots: forms in and- (probably from Vulgar Latin *ambitāre, frequentative of ambīre, 'to go around') and singular/3rd-plural present vad-/va- from Latin vādere.

anello.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ānellus ('little ring, signet ring'), diminutive of ānus ('ring, circle').

angolo.etymology: Semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin angŭlus ('corner, angle, nook').

anno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin annus, annum ('year, annual cycle').

annuale.etymology: Continues Late Latin annuālis ('yearly, annual'), extended from Classical Latin annuus (derived from annus, 'year').

anticipo.etymology: Deverbal back-formation from anticipare ('to anticipate, do or pay in advance'), itself borrowed from Classical Latin anticipāre (compound of ante- 'before' + capĕre 'to take').

history.meaning: to do in advance -> advance, earliness (in anticipo)

antico.etymology: Continues Classical Latin antīquus ('ancient, old, former, of old'), derived from ante ('before, in front').

anziano.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *anteānus ('prior, older, elder'), derived from Latin ante ('before') + the suffix -ānus, with regular palatalization of -ti- to -zi-.

aperto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin apertus ('open, uncovered, clear'), past participle of aperīre ('to open, uncover').

apertura.etymology: Continues Classical Latin apertūra ('opening, aperture'), derived from apertus (past participle of aperīre, 'to open').

appartenere.etymology: Continues Late Latin appartinēre ('to belong to, pertain to'), intensive compound of ad- + Classical Latin pertinēre ('to reach to, belong to, concern', from per- + tenēre, 'to hold').

appena.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase a pena (< Latin ad poenam, literally 'with pain/difficulty, scarcely, barely'), extended temporally to mean 'just now, as soon as'.

appendere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin appendĕre ('to hang up, suspend, weigh out'), compound of ad- ('to, upon') + pendĕre ('to hang, weigh').

appiccicoso.etymology: Adjective derived from appiccicare ('to stick, glue', expressive iterative of appiccare, related to pece < Latin pix, pĭcis, 'pitch, tar') + the suffix -oso.

appoggiare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *appodiāre ('to prop up, lean upon, support'), parasynthetic verb formed from ad- + Latin podium ('pedestal, elevated base, hillock', from Ancient Greek πόδιον, pódion).

history.meaning: to lean, rest, put down, support

appunto.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase a punto ('to the point, precisely, at the right moment'), from a (< Latin ad) + punto (< Latin punctum, 'point, prick').

aprire.etymology: Continues syncopated Latin aperīre ('to open, uncover'), with past participle aperto continuing apertus.

arancia.etymology: Borrowed in medieval Italy from Arabic نَارَنْج (nāranj, 'bitter orange'), from Persian nārang < Sanskrit nāraṅga; initial n- (retained in Venetian naranza and Spanish naranja) dropped by rebracketing with the indefinite article (un'arancia) and folk-etymological association with oro ('gold', aurantia).

history.meaning: bitter orange (< Persian nārang < Sanskrit nāraṅga)

architetto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin architectus ('master builder, architect'), from Ancient Greek ἀρχιτέκτων (arkhitéktōn, compound of ἀρχι- arkhi- 'chief, master' + τέκτων téktōn 'builder, carpenter').

arco.etymology: Continues Classical Latin arcus, arcum ('bow, arch, vault, rainbow').

argento.etymology: Continues Classical Latin argentum ('silver, silver plate, money'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erǵ-n̥-tom ('shining white metal').

aria.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *aria, reshaped from Classical Latin accusative āĕra / plural āĕrēs ('air, atmosphere'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, 'lower air, mist, breeze').

armadio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin armārium ('chest, cupboard, closet', originally a repository for arma, 'tools, gear, weapons'), with dissimilation/alteration of the second -r- to -d- (armario > armadio).

arrabbiato.etymology: Participial adjective from arrabbiare ('to become rabid or furious'), continuing Vulgar Latin *arrabiāre (from ad- + Classical Latin rabiēs, 'rage, fury, madness').

arrendersi.etymology: Reflexive form of arrendere ('to hand over, yield'), formed from a- (< Latin ad-) + rendere ('to give back, yield', < Vulgar Latin *rendĕre, reshaped from Classical Latin reddĕre after prendĕre).

history.meaning: to give back, yield (< Classical reddĕre)
to hand over -> to surrender, give up

arrivare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *arrīpāre ('to reach the riverbank or shore, come to land'), parasynthetic verb from ad- ('to') + rīpa ('bank, shore'), reinforced in early Italian by Old French ariver and Old Occitan aribar.

arrivederci.etymology: Compound of a ('until, to') + rivedere ('to see again', re- + vedere from Latin vidēre) + reciprocal pronoun ci ('each other'): literally 'until seeing each other again'.

arrostito.etymology: Participial adjective from arrostire ('to roast'), formed from a- (< Latin ad-) + Germanic (Lombardic or Frankish) *raustjan ('to roast on a gridiron').

articolo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin articŭlus ('little joint, knuckle; clause, point, grammatical article'), diminutive of artus ('joint, limb').

history.meaning: joint -> small joint, subdivision, clause, article

asciugamano.etymology: Verb-noun compound formed within Italian from asciugare ('to dry, wipe dry', 3rd-person singular stem asciuga-) + mano ('hand', < Latin manus), literally 'wipe-hand'.

asciugare.etymology: Continues Late Latin exsūcāre ('to squeeze out the juice or moisture, drain dry'), parasynthetic verb from ex- ('out') + sūcus ('juice, sap, moisture'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of ex-s- to sci- and voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

history.meaning: to drain of moisture, dry out

asciugatura.etymology: Action noun derived within Italian from asciugare ('to dry') + the suffix -tura (< Latin -tūra).

asciutto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin exsūctus ('sucked dry, drained of moisture'), past participle of exsūgĕre ('to suck out', from ex- + sūgĕre), serving as the adjective 'dry' and suppletive participle alongside asciugare.

history.meaning: to suck out -> sucked dry, parched

ascoltare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin ascultāre (attested in Roman inscriptions for Classical Latin auscultāre, 'to listen attentively, lend an ear', with regular dissimilation of initial au- to a- before a following syllable containing u).

aspettare.etymology: Continues Latin exspectāre ('to look out for, await'), crossed in spoken Latin with aspectāre ('to watch attentively').

assaggiare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- (< Latin ad-) + saggio ('test, sample, assay', < Late Latin exagium, 'weighing, balance, trial'), meaning 'to test, sample, taste'.

assaggiatore.etymology: Agent noun derived within Italian from assaggiare ('to taste, sample') + the agent suffix -tore (< Latin -tōrem).

assoluto.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin absolūtus ('loosened, unrestricted, complete, unconditional'), past participle of absolvĕre ('to untie, set free, complete', from ab- + solvĕre).

history.meaning: to set free, complete -> unrestricted, absolute

assumere.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin assūmĕre ('to take to oneself, adopt, take on'), compound of ad- ('to') + sūmĕre ('to take up').

history.meaning: to hire, employ, assume, take on

attaccare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- (< Latin ad-) + tacca ('notch, peg, clasp', of Germanic origin, cf. Lombardic taikn / Proto-Germanic *takkō, 'point, spike, clasp'), originally meaning 'to fasten to a peg or clasp' (the military sense 'to attack' developed in 16th-century Italian from 'to join battle', whence French attaquer).

attentamente.etymology: Adverb formed from the feminine adjective attenta ('attentive, careful', < Latin attentus) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente, 'with an [attentive] mind').

attento.etymology: Continues Classical Latin attentus ('stretched toward, attentive, heedful, careful'), participial adjective of attendĕre ('to stretch toward, direct the mind to', from ad- + tendĕre).

history.meaning: to direct the mind toward -> attentive, careful

attenzione.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin attentiō, attentiōnem ('application of the mind, attentiveness'), derived from attendĕre ('to direct one's mind toward').

attesa.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of attendere ('to wait for, expect', < Classical Latin attendĕre, 'to direct one's mind toward'), modeled on Vulgar Latin *attēnsa (sigmatic past participle for Classical attenta).

history.meaning: to direct the mind toward, pay heed

attimo.etymology: Popular Tuscan adaptation of Classical Latin atŏmus ('indivisible particle; twinkling of an eye, instant in time', from Ancient Greek ἄτομος, átomos, 'uncut, indivisible'), with shift to the proparoxytonic ending -imo.

history.meaning: in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye

attraversare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- (< Latin ad-) + traverso ('crosswise, oblique', < Latin transversus), parallel to Old French atraveser.

attraverso.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase a traverso ('across, crosswise'), from a (< Latin ad) + traverso (< Classical Latin transversus, past participle of transvertĕre, 'to turn across').

attrezzo.etymology: Deverbal back-formation from attrezzare ('to equip, rig'), adapted from Old French atrecier / atillier (ultimately from Vulgar Latin *addirectiāre, 'to set in order, arrange, prepare').

autista.etymology: Coined in 20th-century Italian from auto(mobile) ('car') + the occupational suffix -ista (proposed by Bruno Migliorini in 1932 to replace the French loanword chauffeur).

autunno.etymology: Learned and semi-popular continuation of Latin autumnus ('autumn, harvest season'), with assimilation of -mn- > -nn-.

avanzare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *abantiāre ('to move forward, put ahead, remain over'), derived from Late Latin abante ('in front, before', from ab + ante).

history.meaning: to advance, move forward; to be left over

avere.etymology: Continues Latin habēre ('to hold, possess, have'), developing both possession/idiomatic senses and auxiliary duty in compound past tenses.

avvicinare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from a- (< Latin ad-) + vicino ('near, neighboring', < Classical Latin vīcīnus, from vīcus, 'quarter, village') + -are, with syntactic gemination of -v-.

avviso.etymology: Borrowed from or modeled on Old French avis ('opinion, view, notice', from the phrase ce m'est a vis < Latin mihi est vīsum, 'it seems to me'), or deverbal from avvisare.

avvocato.etymology: Continues Classical Latin advocātus ('one summoned to give legal counsel or aid, advocate'), substantivized past participle of advocāre ('to call to one's aid', from ad- + vocāre).

history.meaning: to summon to aid -> legal counselor, advocate

avvolgere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin adhaerēre-type compound advolvĕre ('to roll toward, wind around'), compound of ad- ('to') + volvĕre ('to roll, turn, wrap'), with regular assimilation of -dv- to -vv-.

azzurro.etymology: Entered Medieval Italian via Arabic lāzaward and Persian lāžward ('lapis lazuli'), with loss of initial l- reinterpreted as the romance definite article.

bacheca.etymology: Originally meaning a goldsmith's glass display case for trinkets, of uncertain origin: either from Late Latin *bacca / bāca ('pearl, bead, berry') or related to medieval dialectal words for a small chest or box (cf. bachiocco / bacca).

bagnare.etymology: Continues Late Latin balneāre (Vulgar Latin *baneāre, 'to bathe, wet'), denominative verb derived from Classical Latin balneum / Vulgar Latin *baneum ('bath').

bagnato.etymology: Participial adjective from bagnare ('to wet, bathe', < Late Latin balneāre / *baneāre), meaning 'wet, soaked'.

bagno.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *baneum, reduced from Classical Latin balneum ('bath, bathhouse'), itself borrowed from Ancient Greek βαλανεῖον (balaneîon, 'bath, bathing room').

banco.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Germanic (Lombardic or Frankish) *bank ('bench, long seat, counter', from Proto-Germanic *bankiz), originally designating a wooden bench and later a moneychanger's counter.

bancone.etymology: Augmentative of banco ('bench, counter', < Germanic *bank) formed with the suffix -one (< Latin -ō, -ōnem), designating a large shop, bar, or workshop counter.

barattolo.etymology: Of uncertain origin, documented in Tuscan since the 14th century; usually connected either with baratto ('exchange, apothecary's trade') or with Late Greek/Medieval Latin *pyxidula / *veratrum or pre-Roman substrate terms for small cylindrical vessels.

base.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin basis ('pedestal, foundation, base'), borrowed from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis, 'step, pedestal, base', from βαίνειν, baínein, 'to step, go').

basso.etymology: Continues Late Latin bassus ('thickset, short, low in stature', attested first as a Roman cognomen Bassus and in glosses), which replaced Classical Latin humilis in the physical sense 'low'.

bastare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *bastāre ('to suffice, hold up under a load'), either derived from Late Latin *bastum ('pack-saddle, support', < Ancient Greek βαστάζειν, bastázein, 'to bear, carry, support') or directly adapted from Greek.

history.meaning: to hold up, be enough, suffice

battere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *battĕre, reduced from Classical Latin battuĕre ('to beat, strike, pound, fence'), possibly an ancient Gaulish borrowing in Latin.

battuta.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of battere ('to beat, strike', < Vulgar Latin *battĕre < Classical battuĕre), developing senses from 'blow, stroke' to 'musical measure/beat' and 'actor's line, witty remark, quip'.

baule.etymology: Early modern Romance word (parallel to French bahut and Spanish baúl) for a domed wooden travel chest or storage trunk.

beccuccio.etymology: Diminutive of becco ('beak, bill, spout', < Latin beccus, of Gaulish origin) formed with the suffix -uccio, designating a small pouring spout or nozzle.

beh.etymology: Clipped interjectional form (apocope) of bene ('well', < Classical Latin bene), used in conversation as a discourse marker meaning 'well, well then'.

bello.etymology: Continues Classical Latin bellus ('pretty, handsome, fine, charming'), originally a colloquial diminutive *duenelos from bonus (Old Latin duenos, 'good'), which in Vulgar Latin supplanted pulcher.

bene.etymology: Continues Classical Latin bene ('well, rightly'), adverb formed from bonus (Old Latin duenos, 'good').

benissimo.etymology: Absolute superlative of bene ('well'), continuing Classical Latin benissimē (rare/colloquial superlative alongside optimē) or formed in Italian from bene + -issimo.

benvenuto.etymology: Univerbation of the welcoming phrase ben venuto ('well come'), from bene (< Latin bene, 'well') + venuto (past participle of venire < Latin venīre, 'to come'), parallel to French bienvenu.

bere.etymology: Contracted from older Tuscan bevere (< Latin bibere, 'to drink'), whose stem bev- survives throughout the inflected forms (bevo, bevi, bevuto).

bianco.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Germanic (Frankish or Lombardic) *blank ('shining, white, gleaming', from Proto-Germanic *blankaz), displacing Classical Latin albus in everyday Romance speech.

biblioteca.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin bibliothēca ('library, book collection'), from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, compound of βιβλίον biblíon 'book' + θήκη thḗkē 'receptacle, repository').

bicchiere.etymology: Continues Vulgar/Medieval Latin bicārium ('drinking goblet, beaker', related to Late Latin bacar and often connected to Ancient Greek βῖκος, bîkos, 'earthenware wine jar', cross-fertilized with Germanic forms like Old High German behhari).

biglietto.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from French billet ('short note, ticket'), diminutive of Old French bille ('written document, papal bull', altered from Medieval Latin bulla, 'seal, sealed document').

binario.etymology: From Late Latin bīnārius ('consisting of two, paired', from bīnī, 'two by two'), naming the pair of parallel iron rails—and hence a station platform.

biscotto.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin panis biscŏctus ('bread baked twice', bis + cŏctus from cŏquĕre), originally dry ship's rusk baked for long keeping.

bisogno.etymology: Derived from early Romance *bisognare / Old French besoing ('need, necessity'), of Frankish origin (*bisunnia, 'care, urgent need, legal excuse', from bi- + *sunnja, 'care, concern').

bloccare.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–19th centuries from French bloquer ('to blockade,immobilize, block'), derived from bloc ('log, block', from Middle Dutch blok).

blu.etymology: Borrowed in the late 17th–18th century from French bleu ('blue'), itself from Frankish *blāo ('blue, dark-colored', from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz), supplementing traditional Tuscan azzurro and turchino.

bolla.etymology: Continues Classical Latin bulla ('water bubble, boss, stud; papal seal'), with regular lowering of short Latin u to closed o.

bordo.etymology: Entered Italian via Old French bord from Frankish *bord ('ship's side, plank, rim'), cognate with English board.

borsa.etymology: Continues Late Latin bursa ('hide, leather pouch, purse'), borrowed from Ancient Greek βύρσα (býrsa, 'dressed hide, wineskin, leather bag').

borsellino.etymology: Double diminutive of borsa ('bag, purse', < Late Latin bursa) via borsello + -ino, designating a small change purse or coin pouch.

bosco.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin bŭscus / *bŏscus ('woodland, copse'), of West Germanic origin (*busk, cognate with English bush and German Busch).

bottiglia.etymology: Borrowed via Old French bouteille or Spanish botilla from Late Latin buttĭcŭla ('small cask, flask, bottle'), diminutive of Late Latin buttis ('cask, barrel').

botto.etymology: Of expressive/onomatopoeic origin (*bott-*, imitating a sudden dull thud or bang; cf. botta, 'blow, strike' and French bouter), attested since the 13th century.

history.meaning: bang, loud thud, sudden stroke (di botto)

braccio.etymology: Continues Latin brāchĭum ('forearm, arm'), borrowed from Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn); plural le braccia continues the Latin neuter plural brāchĭa.

brano.etymology: Continues early Italian brano ('torn piece of flesh or cloth, shred', later 'excerpt, passage of music or literature'), borrowed via Old French braon ('fleshy part, chunk of meat') from Frankish *brādo ('piece of roast meat, calf muscle').

history.meaning: torn piece, shred -> literary or musical passage

bravo.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *bravus ('untamed, fierce, bold'), most widely explained as a phonetic reduction of Classical Latin barbărus ('foreign, wild, untamed') or pravus ('crooked, unruly'), evolving from 'bold, fearless' to 'skilled, capable, good'.

breve.etymology: Continues Classical Latin brĕvis, brĕvem ('short, brief, small'), from Proto-Indo-European *mregʰ-u- ('short').

brillante.etymology: Participial adjective from brillare ('to shine, sparkle'), also substantivized for a brilliant-cut diamond and figuratively 'brilliant, clever'.

brillare.etymology: Originating in Renaissance Italian (whence French briller), probably derived from Vulgar Latin *beryllāre ('to gleam like a beryl crystal', from Latin bēryllus < Greek βήρυλλος, bḗryllos) or from an expressive root *brill- / *pirl- ('to whirl, quiver, sparkle').

brocca.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *brocca ('jug, pitcher', originally a vessel with a projecting spout or lip), feminine noun from Latin broccus ('projecting, buck-toothed, pointed').

bruciatore.etymology: Agent/instrument noun formed within Italian from bruciare ('to burn', < Vulgar Latin *brūsiāre, a blend of Latin ūstulāre with a Celtic or Germanic root) + the suffix -tore (< Latin -tōrem).

brutto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin brūtus ('heavy, unwieldy, dull, irrational, brutish'), with expressive gemination of -t- in Vulgar Latin (*brūttus), shifting from 'rough, foul, dirty' to 'ugly, bad'.

buccia.etymology: Probably from Late Latin *bŭllĕa or pre-Latin Mediterranean stock crossed with lobia ('pod, husk'), attested in Tuscan since the 14th century for fruit rind and tree bark.

buco.etymology: Probably borrowed from Germanic (Lombardic) *būh ('belly, hollow cavity, trunk', cf. Old High German būh, German Bauch), or from a Vulgar Latin expressive variant of *bucca ('opening, cavity').

buffo.etymology: Of onomatopoeic origin (*buff-*, imitating a puff of wind or puffed-out cheeks, cf. buffare, 'to puff, blow, jest'), developing the sense 'comical, funny, grotesque'.

history.meaning: puff of wind, jest / to puff out cheeks

buio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin bŭrrus ('dark red, russet, dusky', borrowed from Ancient Greek πυρρός, pyrrhós) via a derivative *bŭrĭus ('reddish-dark, murky, gloomy'), with regular Tuscan reduction of -ri- to -i- (as in cuoio < corium).

bum.etymology: Onomatopoeic interjection imitating the deep resonant sound of an explosion, cannon shot, or heavy impact.

buonanotte.etymology: Univerbation of the greeting phrase buona notte ('good night'), from buona (< Latin bŏna, feminine of bŏnus, 'good') + notte (< Latin nox, noctem, 'night').

buonasera.etymology: Compound of buona ('good', f.) + sera ('evening', from Latin sēra [diēs], 'late part of the day').

buongiorno.etymology: Univerbation of buon ('good', from Latin bonus) + giorno ('day', from Late Latin diurnum), literally wishing someone a good day.

buono.etymology: Continues Classical Latin bŏnus, bŏnum ('good', Old Latin duenos), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short Latin ŏ in an open syllable to uo.

burro.etymology: Via Old French burre from Latin būtyrum and Ancient Greek boútyron ('cow-cheese'); replaced older Tuscan butirro in everyday Italian.

bussare.etymology: Either continuing Late Latin *pulsāre (with labial assimilation *bussāre, from Classical pulsāre, 'to beat, knock at a door') or formed from an expressive/onomatopoeic root *buss-* imitating a knock.

busta.etymology: Derived via northern Italian and French boîte / Old French boiste from Late Latin buxĭda (accusative of buxis, 'small boxwood case', borrowed from Ancient Greek πυξίς, pyxís, 'boxwood receptacle'), shifting from 'small case for cutlery or papers' to 'paper envelope, plastic bag'.

buttare.etymology: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from Old French bouter / Old Occitan botar ('to strike, push, thrust, throw'), itself from Frankish *bōtan ('to strike, beat, push', from Proto-Germanic *bautaną).

cacciavite.etymology: Verb-noun compound formed within Italian from cacciare ('to drive in, push, force', 3rd-person singular stem caccia-) + vite ('screw', < Latin vītis, 'vine tendril, spiral screw').

cadere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *cadēre, shifted to the second conjugation from Classical Latin cadĕre ('to fall, drop, sink').

caffè.etymology: Entered Italian (first through Venice in the late sixteenth century) from Ottoman Turkish kahve and Arabic qahwa, naming both the roasted bean drink and the coffeehouse.

calante.etymology: Participial adjective from the present participle of calare ('to lower, go down, wane', < Late Latin chalāre), meaning 'waning, decreasing, flat (in pitch)'.

history.meaning: to drop, wane -> waning, falling, slightly flat

calare.etymology: Continues Late Latin chalāre ('to slacken, lower a sail or net, let down'), borrowed from Ancient Greek χαλάω (khaláō, 'to slacken, loosen, let down').

history.meaning: to lower, go down, drop, decrease

caldaia.etymology: Continues Late Latin caldāria ('cauldron, pot for boiling water, hot bath'), substantivized feminine of Classical Latin caldārius ('pertaining to warming', from calĭdus / caldus, 'hot'), with regular Tuscan evolution of -ria to -ia.

caldo.etymology: Continues syncopated Latin caldus for classical calidus ('warm, hot', related to calēre), already noted by Roman grammarians as everyday spoken Latin.

calligrafia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Greek καλλιγραφία (kalligraphía, 'beautiful writing'), compound of κάλλος (kállos, 'beauty', from καλός, 'beautiful') + -γραφία (-graphía, 'writing', from γράφειν, 'to write').

calma.etymology: Continues Late Latin cauma ('burning heat of the midday sun', when wind dies down and activity ceases at sea), borrowed from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, 'burning heat', from καίειν, kaíein, 'to burn'), with change of au > al before a labial consonant.

calmo.etymology: Adjective derived from calma ('calmness, windless lull', < Late Latin cauma < Greek kaûma) or back-formed from calmare ('to calm').

calore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin calor, calōrem ('warmth, heat, glow, ardor'), built on the stem of calēre ('to be warm or hot').

cambiare.etymology: Continues Late Latin cambiāre ('to exchange, barter'), a Latin borrowing from Gaulish *kambiom / *kambjāre ('to exchange, bend, turn back', from Proto-Celtic *kambos).

cambio.etymology: Deverbal noun from cambiare ('to change, exchange', < Late Latin cambiāre) or continuing Late Latin cambium ('exchange, barter', of Gaulish origin).

camera.etymology: From Latin camera (borrowed from Ancient Greek kamára, 'vaulted chamber, arched roof'), shifting to mean a private room or hotel bedroom.

camicia.etymology: Continues Late Latin camīsia ('linen shirt or nightgown', recorded by St. Jerome in the 4th century as a soldier's close-fitting linen tunic), borrowed into Latin from Gaulish or Germanic (cf. Proto-Germanic *hamiþiją, 'shirt').

camion.etymology: Borrowed in the early 20th century from French camion ('heavy dray, wagon, truck'), from northern French/Norman-Picard kamion (14th c.), of uncertain origin.

camminare.etymology: From Late Latin cammināre ('to travel along a road, walk'), a denominal verb derived from Vulgar Latin cammīnus ('way, path'), borrowed from Gaulish *camminos ('step, way').
camminare.notes: Cognate with French cheminer and Spanish caminar; replaced Classical Latin ambulāre as the everyday Italian verb for walking.

cammino.etymology: From Vulgar Latin cammīnus ('way, road, path'), borrowed from Gaulish *camminos ('step, journey'), from Proto-Celtic *kanxsman ('step').
cammino.notes: Masculine noun (il cammino, 'path, journey'); the 1st-person present form of camminare ('io cammino') shares its spelling.

camomilla.etymology: Continues Late Latin chamomĭlla (alteration of chamaemēlon), from Greek χαμαίμηλον (khamaímēlon, 'earth-apple', named for the apple-like scent of its blossoms).

campanello.etymology: Diminutive of campana ('bell', from Late Latin campāna [vasa], 'Campanian bronze vessels/bells', named after Campania, renowned for bronze casting) formed with the masculine diminutive suffix -ello.

campanile.etymology: Derived within Italian from campana ('church bell', < Late Latin campāna) + the locative/relational suffix -ile (< Latin -īle), designating a freestanding or attached bell tower.

cancello.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cancellus (mostly plural cancellī, 'lattice, grating, bars, barrier', diminutive of cancer, 'crab; lattice'), whence both 'iron gate' and 'chancery'.

cannella.etymology: Diminutive of canna ('reed, cane, tube', < Latin canna < Greek kánna, of Semitic origin), formed with -ella because dried cinnamon bark curls into small hollow reed-like quills (also used for a small water tap or spout).

history.meaning: little reed, small tube; rolled quill of cinnamon bark

cantabile.etymology: Continues Late Latin cantābĭlis ('worthy to be sung, songlike'), derived from cantāre ('to sing'); internationally adopted from Italian as a musical performance term meaning 'in a singing, melodious style'.

cantare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cantāre ('to sing, chant'), originally the frequentative/intensive verb of canĕre ('to sing') which completely replaced the simple verb in Romance.

history.meaning: to sing -> to sing repeatedly, chant

canticchiare.etymology: Attenuative/frequentative verb formed within Italian from cantare ('to sing', < Latin cantāre) with the suffix -icchiare (< Vulgar Latin *-iculāre), meaning 'to hum, croon softly'.

history.meaning: to hum, sing softly to oneself

cantina.etymology: Derived within Italian (probably from canto, 'corner, secluded nook', with suffix -ina) to name a cool underground storage cellar or wine cellar.

canzone.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cantiō, cantiōnem ('song, singing, incantation', derived from canĕre / cantāre), influenced in its early lyric sense by Old Occitan canso.

capitare.etymology: Continues Medieval/Vulgar Latin *capitāre ('to come to a head, arrive at a destination, happen to turn up'), derived from Classical Latin caput, capĭtis ('head, end, point').

history.meaning: to arrive at a place, turn up
to happen, occur, turn up by chance

capo.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *capum, regularized masculine accusative of Classical Latin neuter caput ('head, top, extremity, leader').

cappotto.etymology: Augmentative/derivative of cappa ('hooded cloak, cape', < Late Latin cappa) formed with the suffix -otto, designating a heavy overcoat.

cardigan.etymology: Borrowed from English cardigan ('knitted buttoned jacket or sweater'), named after James Thomas Brudenell, 7th Earl of Cardigan (1797–1868), who led the Charge of the Light Brigade during the Crimean War.

history.meaning: buttoned knitted sweater (from the 7th Earl of Cardigan)

cardine.etymology: Continues Latin cardō, cardĭnis ('door pivot, hinge, pole of the sky'), from the accusative cardĭnem.

carino.etymology: Diminutive/endearing adjective derived within Italian from caro ('dear, beloved', < Classical Latin cārus) + the diminutive suffix -ino.

caro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cārus ('dear, precious, costly, beloved'), from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂-ro- ('desired, loved').

carota.etymology: Continues Latin carōta ('carrot'), borrowed from Greek καρωτόν (karōtón).

carta.etymology: Continues Classical Latin charta ('leaf of papyrus, sheet of paper, document'), borrowed from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, 'roll or sheet of papyrus').

carteggiare.etymology: Denominative verb formed within Italian from carta ('paper, sandpaper, letter', < Latin charta) + -eggiare, meaning both 'to sand down with sandpaper (carta vetrata)' and 'to exchange letters, correspond'.

history.meaning: to sand, smooth with sandpaper; to correspond

cartella.etymology: Diminutive formation in -ella on Italian carta ('paper, document', < Latin charta < Greek χάρτης, khártēs, 'papyrus sheet').

cartelletta.etymology: Diminutive of cartella ('folder, briefcase, satchel', itself a diminutive/derivative of carta, 'paper') formed with the suffix -etta, designating a thin file folder.

history.meaning: paper -> folder, satchel -> file folder, document sleeve

cartellino.etymology: Diminutive of cartello ('placard, sign', from carta, 'paper, card') formed with -ino, designating a small tag, price tag, label, or timecard.

history.meaning: paper -> sign, notice -> small tag, label, badge

cartello.etymology: Derived within Italian from carta ('paper, sheet', < Latin charta) + the suffix -ello, originally a public notice or written challenge posted on a wall, now 'sign, placard, road sign' (and in economics 'cartel').

cartolina.etymology: Diminutive derived from carta ('paper, card') via cartola + -ina, coined in the late 19th century (cartolina postale) for a postcard.

cartoncino.etymology: Diminutive of cartone ('cardboard, pasteboard', augmentative of carta) formed with -cino, designating light cardstock, bristol board, or a small card.

history.meaning: paper -> heavy cardboard -> cardstock, thin cardboard

cartone.etymology: Augmentative of carta ('paper', < Latin charta) formed with the suffix -one, originally designating heavy pasteboard or a full-scale preparatory drawing for a fresco (whence English cartoon), and later 'cardboard, carton'.

history.meaning: cardboard, carton; preparatory drawing, animated cartoon

casa.etymology: Continues Latin casa (originally a modest 'cottage, hut'), which supplanted classical domus across Romance languages as the general word for house and home.

caso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cāsus, cāsum ('fall, chance, accident, event, grammatical case'), action noun from cadĕre ('to fall, happen').

history.meaning: to fall -> fall, chance occurrence, case

cassa.etymology: Continues Classical Latin capsa ('box, chest, cylindrical case for book rolls', related to capĕre, 'to hold, contain'), with regular assimilation of -ps- to -ss-.

history.meaning: box, crate, chest, cash desk, checkout

cassetta.etymology: Diminutive of cassa ('box, chest', < Classical Latin capsa) formed with the feminine suffix -etta, designating a small box, crate, mailbox, or tape cassette.

cassetto.etymology: Masculine diminutive of cassa ('box, chest', < Classical Latin capsa) formed with -etto, specialized in Italian for a sliding 'drawer' in a piece of furniture.

cattivo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin captīvus ('taken prisoner, captive', from capĕre, 'to take') via Christian Late Latin captīvus diabŏlī ('prisoner of the devil', hence 'wretched, wicked, bad, evil'), with regular assimilation of -pt- to -tt-.

caviglia.etymology: Through Old Provençal cavilha from Vulgar Latin *clavĭcŭla (for Classical clavīcŭla, 'small peg or bolt', diminutive of clāvis), applied anatomically to the anklebone.

cedere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cēdĕre ('to go, withdraw, yield, give way, grant').

history.meaning: to yield, give in, give way, transfer

cedro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cedrus ('cedar tree; citron tree'), borrowed from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros, 'cedar; citron').

cena.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cēna ('main afternoon or evening meal, dinner'), from Old Latin cesna < Proto-Italic *kertsnā ('portion, meal').

centesimo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin centēsimus ('hundredth'), ordinal numeral derived from centum ('hundred').

history.meaning: hundredth; cent (one-hundredth of a currency unit)

centimetro.etymology: Learned metric compound borrowed via French centimètre (1795), from Latin centum ('hundred') + Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure').

cento.etymology: Continues Classical Latin centum ('one hundred'), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm ('hundred').

centrale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin centrālis ('in the middle, central'), derived from centrum ('center').

centro.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin centrum ('stationary point of a compass, center of a circle'), borrowed from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, 'sharp point, goad, stationary pivot of a pair of compasses').

history.meaning: sharp point, pivot of a compass, center

ceramica.etymology: Borrowed via French céramique from Greek κεραμική (τέχνη) (keramikḗ, 'potter's art'), from κέραμος (kéramos, 'potter's clay, earthenware').

cercare.etymology: Continues Late Latin circāre ('to go around, wander through, traverse in search of'), denominative verb from Classical Latin circus / circa ('circle, around').

history.meaning: to go around, patrol, search through

cerchiare.etymology: Denominative verb from cerchio ('circle, hoop, rim', < Classical Latin circŭlus, diminutive of circus, with regular evolution of -cl- to -chi-).

cerniera.etymology: Borrowed from Old French charniere ('hinge, pivot'), continuing Late Latin *cardĭnāria from Latin cardō, cardĭnis ('door pivot, hinge').

certo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin certus ('resolved, determined, sure, certain'), originally an old participial adjective of cernĕre ('to sift, distinguish, decide').

history.meaning: to sift, decide -> decided, sure, certain

cessione.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin cessiō, cessiōnem ('a yielding up, legal transfer, assignment of rights'), derived from cēdĕre ('to yield, transfer', past participle cessus).

history.meaning: to yield, transfer -> legal surrender, transfer
transfer, assignment, conveyance (of property or lease)

cestino.etymology: Diminutive of cesto / cesta ('basket', < Classical Latin cista, 'woven box or basket', borrowed from Ancient Greek κίστη, kístē) formed with -ino, designating a small basket or wastepaper bin.

cesto.etymology: Continues Latin cĭsta ('woven basket, chest'), borrowed from Greek κίστη (kístē, 'wicker basket').

che.etymology: Confluence in Vulgar Latin and early Italian of Classical Latin quid ('what?', interrogative/indefinite pronoun), quem / quae (relative pronoun), and quia / quod ('that, because', conjunction).

check-in.etymology: Unadapted 20th-century borrowing from English check-in (noun conversion of the phrasal verb to check in, 'to register one's arrival at a hotel or airport').

history.meaning: to register arrival -> registration at a hotel or airport

chi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quī ('who, whoever; he who'), nominative masculine singular interrogative and relative pronoun.

chiacchierata.etymology: Action noun formed from the feminine past participle of chiacchierare ('to chat, chatter'), itself of expressive/onomatopoeic origin (*chiacch- / *klakk-, imitating lively chatter).

chiamare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin clāmāre ('to cry out, shout, proclaim, call upon'), with regular Tuscan evolution of initial cl- to chi- (/kj/).

chiaramente.etymology: Adverb formed from the feminine adjective chiara ('clear, bright', < Classical Latin clāra) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente).

chiaro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin clārus ('bright, shining, clear, loud, famous'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial cl- to chi- (/kj/).

chiave.etymology: Continues Latin clāvem (accusative of clāvis, 'key', related to claudere, 'to close'), with regular Italian palatalization of initial cl- > chi- (/kj/).

chiavistello.etymology: Tuscan alteration (crossed with chiave, 'key') of Vulgar Latin *clāvicĕllus, diminutive of Latin clāvis ('key, locking bar').

chiedere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin quaerĕre ('to seek, look for, ask, inquire'), with dissimilation of the first r to d (*quaedĕre) in Vulgar Latin.

chilo.etymology: Shortening of chilogrammo, borrowed from French kilogramme (1795), coined from Greek χίλιοι (khílioi, 'thousand') + γράμμα (grámma, 'gram, small weight').

chiudere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *clūdere (modelled on compounds like inclūdere, exclūdere from classical claudere, 'to close'), with regular cl- > chi-.

chiuso.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *clūsus (from compound forms like inclūsus, exclūsus) for Classical Latin clausus ('shut, closed'), past participle of claudĕre / *clūdĕre ('to close, shut'), with regular initial cl- > chi-.

ci.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(ec)ce hīc ('right here, in this place'), which yielded Old Italian ci ('here, there', locative clitic) and subsequently generalized in Tuscan as the unstressed first-person plural pronoun ('us, to us', replacing older ne < Latin nōs).

history.meaning: there, here; us, to us, ourselves

ciao.etymology: Borrowed from Venetian s-ciao / s-ciavo ('[your] servant'), from Medieval Latin sclavus; generalized across Italy as an informal greeting for both hello and goodbye.

cielo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin caelum ('sky, heaven, vault of heaven'), monophthongized in Vulgar Latin to open *cɛlu and diphthongized in Tuscan to cielo.

cima.etymology: Continues Late/Vulgar Latin cȳma ('young sprout of a cabbage or plant, top shoot, summit'), borrowed from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kŷma, 'swelling, wave, young sprout of a plant').

history.meaning: top shoot of a plant, summit

cinquanta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *cinquanta, dissimilated from Classical Latin quīnquāgintā ('fifty') on analogy with cinque (< *cinque for quīnque).

cinque.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *cinque, formed by regressive dissimilation of the first labiovelar from Classical Latin quīnque ('five').

ciotola.etymology: Attested in Tuscan since the 14th century, probably a metathesized or expressive variant connected to Late Latin cotŭla / cotȳla ('small cup, bowl, liquid measure', from Ancient Greek κοτύλη, kotýlē) crossed with ciottolo.

ciottolo.etymology: Attested in Tuscan since the 14th century for a smooth rounded river stone or cobblestone; of expressive or pre-Roman substrate origin (*ciott-*, evoking a rounded lump or the clatter of stones).

cittadina.etymology: Derived within Italian from cittadino ('citizen, town-dwelling', from città < Latin cīvitās + -ino < -īnus), used as a feminine noun for both 'female citizen' and 'small town, country town'.

città.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cīvitās, cīvitātem ('citizenship, community of citizens; in Late Latin, city, replacing urbs'), via Old Italian cittade with apocope of the final syllable after the dental stop.

clic.etymology: Onomatopoeic noun and interjection imitating the sharp metallic sound of a latch, switch, camera shutter, or computer mouse button (reinforced by French clic and English click).

codardo.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Old French coart ('cowardly, timid', derived from coe < Latin cauda, 'tail', + pejorative suffix -art, originally referring to an animal with its tail tucked between its legs in fear).

history.meaning: turning tail, with tail between legs, cowardly

col.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of con ('with', < Latin cum) + the masculine singular definite article il (via Old Italian co lo > col, from Latin cum illō).

colazione.etymology: From Latin collātiōnem ('bringing together, monastic light meal read aloud together'), shifting in modern standard Italian to mean breakfast (prima colazione).

colla.etymology: Continues Late Latin cŏlla ('glue, paste'), borrowed from Greek κόλλα (kólla, 'hide or fish glue').

collegare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin colligāre ('to bind together, tie up, connect, unite'), compound of com- ('together') + ligāre ('to tie, bind').

collina.etymology: Continues Latin collīna ('hilly ground, small hill'), feminine substantivisation of collīnus from cŏllis ('hill').

colonna.etymology: Continues Classical Latin colŭmna ('pillar, column, post'), related to colŭmen / culmen ('top, gable, supporting pillar'), with regular assimilation of -mn- to -nn- and lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

colore.etymology: Continues Latin colōr, colōrem ('hue, complexion, colour').

colpa.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cŭlpa ('fault, blame, guilt, error'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

colpire.etymology: Denominative verb formed within Italian from colpo ('blow, stroke, hit', < Late Latin colăphus) + -ire, meaning 'to strike, hit, impress'.

colpo.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *colpus, syncopated from Classical/Late Latin colăphus ('blow with the fist, cuff, punch'), borrowed from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos, 'buffet, slap, punch').

coltivare.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin cultivāre ('to till, cultivate'), built on Late Latin cultīvus ('arable, tilled', from Classical Latin cultus, past participle of colĕre, 'to till, tend, inhabit').

come.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *quōmodo et ('in what manner also, just as, how'), reduced from Classical Latin quōmodo ('in what way, how', ablative of quī + modus) + et.

commerciale.etymology: Derived from commercio ('commerce, trade', learned borrowing from Classical Latin commercium, from com- + merx, mercis, 'merchandise') + -ale (modeled in the 18th century on French commercial and English commercial).

commesso.etymology: Substantivized past participle of commettere (< Classical Latin committĕre, 'to entrust, assign a commission or duty'); originally an agent entrusted with business (commesso viaggiatore), now 'shop assistant, sales clerk'.

history.meaning: to entrust -> entrusted with a task

completamente.etymology: Adverb formed from the feminine adjective completa ('complete, full', < Classical Latin complētus) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente).

complimento.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Spanish cumplimiento ('fulfillment of courtesy, polite act or expression', from cumplir < Latin complēre, 'to fill up, fulfill what is due in politeness'), whence Italian passed the word to French compliment and English compliment.

comporre.etymology: Continues Latin compōnĕre ('to put together, arrange, write music or verse'), syncopated in Tuscan to comporre like porre < pōnĕre.

compositrice.etymology: Feminine agent noun corresponding to compositore, continuing Late Latin compositrix, compositrīcem (feminine of compositor, 'one who puts together, arranger, author', from compōnĕre, 'to put together, compose').

comprare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin comparāre ('to prepare, procure, furnish, purchase'), with syncope of the unstressed pretonic vowel (*comprāre); originally 'to get ready, acquire', which in Italian and Iberian Romance displaced emĕre ('to buy').

compratore.etymology: Continues Classical/Late Latin comparātor, comparātōrem ('purchaser, buyer', derived from comparāre) or formed within Italian from comprare ('to buy') + -tore.

computer.etymology: Unadapted 20th-century borrowing from English computer ('electronic data-processing machine'), derived from to compute (< Latin computāre, 'to reckon, calculate together', from com- + putāre).

comunale.etymology: Continues Late/Medieval Latin commūnālis ('shared by the community, municipal'), derived from Classical Latin commūnis ('common, shared') and linked in Italy to the medieval comune ('municipality').

comune.etymology: Continues Classical Latin commūnis ('common, public, shared by all', from com- + mūnus, 'duty, public service'); substantivized in medieval Italy (il comune) for the self-governing city-state and modern municipality ('town hall, municipality').

comunque.etymology: Univerbation of Old Italian come unque ('however, in whatever way'), modeled on Latin quōmodocumque from come ('how', < quōmodo et) + unque ('ever', < Latin unquam).

con.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cum ('with, together with'), with regular loss of final -m and lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

concerto.etymology: Deverbal noun from concertare ('to harmonize, agree together, arrange'), continuing Late Latin concertāre ('to contend, debate', reanalyzed in Renaissance Italian through association with conserĕre, 'to entwine, join together', as 'to bring voices or instruments into harmony').

history.meaning: to contend -> to bring into agreement, harmonize
to harmonize -> musical concert, concerto, agreement

confrontare.etymology: Continues Medieval Latin confrontāre ('to border upon, set face to face, compare'), parasynthetic verb formed from com- ('together') + frōns, frontis ('forehead, front, brow').

history.meaning: to set brow to brow, compare

confusione.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin confūsiō, confūsiōnem ('a mingling together, disorder, confusion, blushing'), derived from confundĕre ('to pour together, mingle, throw into disorder').

history.meaning: to pour together -> mingling, disorder, confusion

conoscere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cognōscĕre ('to become acquainted with, learn, recognize, know'), compound of co- ('together') + (g)nōscĕre ('to come to know'), with dissimilatory reduction of -gn- before palatal -sc-.

history.meaning: to get to know, recognize, know
to know, be acquainted with, meet

consegnare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin consignāre ('to seal, attest with a seal, record, hand over formally'), compound of com- + signāre ('to mark, seal', from signum).

consumare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin consūmĕre ('to use up, eat up, waste, destroy', from com- + sūmĕre), shifted to the first conjugation through conflation in Late Latin with consummāre ('to sum up, complete, consummate', from summa).

history.meaning: to use up, spend, wear out
to consume, use up, wear out

contaminuti.etymology: Verb-noun compound formed in 20th-century Italian from contare ('to count', 3rd-person singular stem conta-) + minuti ('minutes', plural of minuto), literally 'count-minutes'.

contante.etymology: Substantivized present participle of contare ('to count out coins, reckon', < Late Latin computāre), originally in the phrase denaro contante ('money counted out on the spot, ready cash').

continuare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin continuāre ('to join together without interruption, carry on, keep on'), derived from continuus ('uninterrupted, continuous', from continēre, 'to hold together').

history.meaning: to hold together -> continuous -> to continue

contratto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin contractus ('a drawing together; business agreement, bargain, contract'), derived from contrahĕre ('to draw together, conclude a bargain', from com- + trahĕre).

history.meaning: to draw together, conclude a deal -> contract, agreement

contro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin contrā ('against, opposite, facing'), reshaped with final -o on analogy with other disyllabic spatial prepositions/adverbs such as dentro and dietro (while contra survives in compounds).

controllare.etymology: Borrowed via French contrôler ('to verify against a duplicate register, inspect'), derived from Old French contrerolle ('duplicate scroll kept for verification', from contre- 'against' + rolle < Latin rotŭlus, 'scroll, roll').

history.meaning: duplicate register roll used to verify accounts

coperchio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin opercŭlum ('lid, cover', from operīre, 'to cover'), crossed in Vulgar Latin with cooperīre ('to cover completely') to yield *coopercŭlum > *coperc(u)lum, with regular evolution of -cl- to -chi-.

coperta.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of coprire ('to cover', < Classical Latin cooperīre, 'to cover completely', via Vulgar Latin *coperīre), originally 'that which covers'.

coppia.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *cōpla, syncopated from Classical Latin cōpŭla ('band, tie, bond, pair joined together', from co- + apĕre, 'to fasten'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of intervocalic -pl- to -ppi- (compare doppio < duplus).

corda.etymology: Continues Latin chŏrda ('gut string of a lyre; cord'), from Greek χορδή (khordḗ, 'gut, musical string').

correre.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cŭrrĕre ('to run, hasten, flow'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

corridoio.etymology: Derived from correre ('to run', from Latin currere) with the place suffix -toio/-doio: originally a long passage along which one could run between rooms or fortifications.

corsa.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of correre ('to run', < Classical Latin cŭrrĕre, past participle cŭrsus, feminine cŭrsa), designating a run, race, ride, or trip.

cortile.etymology: Derived from corte ('court, enclosed yard', from Latin cohortem / cōrtem) with the suffix -ile, naming the open inner courtyard of an Italian palazzo or inn.

cosa.etymology: Continues Classical Latin causa ('cause, reason, legal case, matter, affair'), which in Late and Vulgar Latin generalized to displace rēs in the sense 'thing, object', with regular monophthongization of au to open o.

costante.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin constāns, constantem ('standing firm, steady, unchanging, faithful'), present participle of constāre ('to stand firm, hold together').

costare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin constāre ('to stand together, stand firm; to stand at a price, cost'), compound of com- + stāre ('to stand'), with regular reduction of -ns- to -s-.

history.meaning: to stand at a price, cost

così.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu(m) sīc ('behold thus, just so'), from Classical Latin eccum ('here is, behold') + sīc ('so, thus').

cravatta.etymology: Adopted in the 17th century (alongside French cravate) from the linen neck-scarves worn by Croatian light cavalrymen (Croatta / Cravatta, from Serbo-Croatian Hrvat, 'Croat') serving in the European wars of the 1600s.

credere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin crēdĕre ('to entrust, trust, believe'), an ancient Indo-European religious compound (*ḱred-dʰeh₁-, literally 'to place one's heart').

crema.etymology: Entered Italian via Old French cresme, blending Late Latin chrisma ('anointing salve', < Greek χρῖσμα) with Gaulish *crama ('milk skimmings').

crepa.etymology: Deverbal noun from crepare ('to crack, burst, split open'), which continues Classical Latin crepāre ('to rattle, crackle, burst with a sharp sound').

history.meaning: to crack, split -> crack, fissure, crevice

crescere.etymology: Continues Latin crēscĕre ('to come into being, grow, increase'), an inchoative verb in -sc-.

croccante.etymology: Participial adjective from croccare ('to crunch, crackle under the teeth'), of onomatopoeic origin (*krokk-*, imitating a crisp crunching sound; compare French croquant).

crosta.etymology: Continues Classical Latin crŭsta ('hard outer surface, rind, bark, shell, scab, bread crust'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

crostata.etymology: Derived within Italian from crosta ('crust, pastry shell', < Classical Latin crŭsta) + -ata, attested since Renaissance cookbooks for an open-faced baked jam or fruit tart with a lattice pastry crust.

history.meaning: baked tart with a pastry crust

crostatina.etymology: Diminutive of crostata ('baked jam or fruit tart', from crosta, 'crust') formed with the diminutive suffix -ina, designating an individual mini-tart.

history.meaning: crust -> jam tart -> small individual tart

cubetto.etymology: Diminutive of cubo ('cube', learned borrowing from Classical Latin cubus < Ancient Greek κύβος, kýbos, 'six-sided die, cube') formed with the suffix -etto.

history.meaning: small cube, ice cube, diced piece

cucchiaino.etymology: Diminutive of cucchiaio ('spoon', < Vulgar Latin *cochleārium, from Classical Latin cochleāre, 'spoon with a pointed handle for eating snails and eggs', from cochlea, 'snail shell') formed with -ino.

cucchiaio.etymology: Continues Latin cochlĕārium ('spoon originally used for eating snails and eggs'), derived from cochlĕa ('snail shell').

cucina.etymology: Continues Late Latin cocīna (attested variant of Classical Latin coquīna, 'kitchen, art of cooking', derived from coquĕre, 'to cook').

cugino.etymology: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from Old French cosin ('cousin'), itself a phonetic reduction of Classical Latin consōbrīnus ('mother's sister's child, first cousin', from com- + soror, 'sister').

cuocere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *cŏcĕre (for Classical Latin cŏquĕre, 'to cook, bake, ripen'), with regular Tuscan diphthongisation of stressed open ŏ.

cuoio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cŏrium ('thick hide, skin, leather'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of short ŏ to uo and palatal reduction of -ri- to -i-.

cuore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cŏr ('heart, mind, spirit'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ŏ in an open syllable to uo.

curare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin cūrāre ('to care for, attend to, treat medically, heal'), denominative verb from cūra ('care, attention, treatment').

history.meaning: care -> to take care of, tend, heal
to care for, look after, treat, cure

curiosare.etymology: Denominative verb formed within Italian from curioso ('curious, inquisitive', < Classical Latin cūriōsus) + -are, meaning 'to browse, snoop around, look around curiously'.

history.meaning: curious -> to browse, poke around, look around

curioso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin cūriōsus ('full of care, painstaking; inquisitive, eager to know, curious'), derived from cūra ('care, attention').

curva.etymology: Substantivized feminine of the adjective curvo ('bent, curved', < Classical Latin curvus, 'crooked, bent, curved'), withlinea ('line') or via ('road') originally understood.

cuscino.etymology: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from Old French coissin / Old Occitan coissi ('cushion, pillow'), from Vulgar Latin *coxīnus ('hip-pad, seat cushion'), derived from Classical Latin coxa ('hip, thigh').

custodire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin custōdīre ('to watch over, guard, protect, keep safe'), denominative verb from custōs, custōdis ('guardian, keeper, watchman').

history.meaning: guardian -> to guard, watch over, keep safe
to guard, keep safe, look after

da.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *da, formed by the compounding and reduction of Classical Latin dē ab ('from away from') or dē ad, uniquely preserved in Italian and Raeto-Romance for origin, agency, and purpose.

history.meaning: from, by, since, at the house/shop of, to (purpose)

dagli.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of da ('from, by', < Vulgar Latin *da) + the masculine plural definite article gli (< Old Italian li < Latin illī); as a verb/interjection, imperative da' (< dare) + gli.

history.meaning: from the, by the (masculine plural before vowel/s+consonant/z)

dai.etymology: Conversational exhortative interjection ('come on!, go on!'), lexicalized from the second-person singular imperative dai / da' of dare ('to give', < Latin dăre); homophonous with the articulated preposition dai (da + i, 'from the').

history.meaning: come on!, go on!; (prep.) from the, by the

dal.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of da ('from, by', < Vulgar Latin *da) + the masculine singular definite article il (via Old Italian da lo > dal).

history.meaning: from the, by the, since the (masculine singular)

dalla.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of da ('from, by', < Vulgar Latin *da) + the feminine singular definite article la (< Latin illam), with regular syntactic gemination of -l-.

dalle.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of da ('from, by', < Vulgar Latin *da) + the feminine plural definite article le (< Latin illās / illae), with regular syntactic gemination of -l-.

dallo.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of da ('from, by', < Vulgar Latin *da) + the masculine singular definite article lo (< Latin illum), with regular syntactic gemination of -l-.

history.meaning: from the, by the (masculine singular before vowel/s+consonant/z)

danzante.etymology: Participial adjective from the present participle of danzare ('to dance'), borrowed in the Middle Ages from Old French dancier (of Frankish origin, cf. *dansōn, 'to draw, stretch out a line of dancers').

dare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dăre ('to give, grant, hand over, offer'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *deh₃- ('to give').

data.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle from the opening Medieval Latin chancery formula data (est epistula) ('[the letter] given [at place and day]', from Classical Latin dătus, past participle of dăre, 'to give').

history.meaning: given (on such a day and at such a place)

davanti.etymology: Univerbation of Vulgar Latin *dē ab ante ('from in front, before'), compound of the Latin prepositions dē + ab + ante (parallel to French devant).

davvero.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase da vero ('in truth, for real, truly'), from da ('from, as') + vero ('true, truth', < Classical Latin vērus), with regular syntactic gemination of -v-.

debole.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dēbĭlis ('maimed, infirm, weak, feeble', from dē- + habĭlis, literally 'unhandy, disabled'), with labialization of the post-tonic vowel before l.

decibel.etymology: Borrowed from international scientific terminology (English decibel, coined in the 1920s at Bell Telephone Laboratories), formed from deci- ('one-tenth', < Latin decimus) + bel (unit of sound intensity named after Alexander Graham Bell, 1847–1922).

history.meaning: one-tenth of a bel (unit named after A. G. Bell)

decisione.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnem ('a cutting off; settlement, agreement, resolution'), derived from dēcīdĕre ('to cut off; to settle, decide', from dē- + caedĕre, 'to cut').

history.meaning: to cut off, settle -> settlement, decision

deciso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin dēcīsus ('cut off; settled, determined, resolved'), past participle of dēcīdĕre (compound of dē- + caedĕre, 'to cut').

history.meaning: to cut off, settle -> decided, determined

degli.etymology: Articulated preposition and partitive article formed by the fusion of di (< Old Italian de < Latin dē, 'of, from') + the masculine plural definite article gli (< Old Italian li < Latin illī).

history.meaning: of the; some (masculine plural before vowel/s+consonant/z)

dei.etymology: Articulated preposition and partitive article formed by the fusion of di (< Old Italian de < Latin dē, 'of, from') + the masculine plural definite article i (reduced from Old Italian li < Latin illī).

del.etymology: Articulated preposition and partitive article formed by the fusion of di (< Old Italian de < Latin dē, 'of, from') + the masculine singular definite article il (via Old Italian de lo > del, from Latin dē illō).

della.etymology: Articulated preposition and partitive article formed by the fusion of di (< Old Italian de < Latin dē, 'of, from') + the feminine singular definite article la (< Latin illam).

delle.etymology: Articulated preposition and partitive article formed by the fusion of di (< Old Italian de < Latin dē, 'of, from') + the feminine plural definite article le (< Latin illās / illae).

dello.etymology: Articulated preposition and partitive article formed by the fusion of di (< Old Italian de < Latin dē, 'of, from') + the masculine singular definite article lo (< Latin illum).

history.meaning: of the; some (masculine singular before vowel/s+consonant/z)

dentro.etymology: Continues Late/Vulgar Latin dē intrō ('from within, on the inside'), compound of Classical Latin dē ('from, of') + intrō ('inward, within').

destra.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dextra (syncopated feminine of dexter, with manus 'hand' or pars 'side' understood), meaning 'right hand, right side'.

destro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dexter, dextĕrum / dextrum ('on the right side, right; skillful, adroit, favorable'), with regular assimilation of -xt- to -st-.

detestare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin dētestārī ('to call down curses upon while invoking the gods as witnesses, execrate, abhor'), deponent compound of dē- + testārī ('to bear witness', from testis, 'witness').

history.meaning: to curse while calling the gods to witness, abhor

di.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dē ('down from, from, concerning, of'), which in Vulgar Latin took over the possessive and partitive functions of the Classical genitive case, with regular raising of unstressed protonic e to i in Tuscan (while de- remains in articulated forms like del, della).

diavolo.etymology: Continues Christian Late Latin diabŏlus ('accuser, slanderer; the Devil'), borrowed from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, 'slanderer, adversary', from διαβάλλειν, diabállein, 'to throw across, traduce, slander').

diciannove.etymology: Continues Late/Vulgar Latin *decem ac novem ('ten and nine', replacing Classical Latin ūndēvīgintī, 'one from twenty'), with palatalization of decem to dici- and syntactic gemination of -n- after ac ('and').

dieci.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dĕcem ('ten'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ĕ to ie and final -i on analogy with other numerals (such as undici, dodici, venti).

dietro.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin dē rĕtrō ('from behind, at the back', compound of Classical Latin dē + rĕtrō, 'backward, behind'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of short ĕ to ie and dissimilatory loss of the first r (*deretro > dietro).

difficile.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin difficĭlis ('hard to do, troublesome, difficult'), negative compound of dis- + facĭlis ('easy to do', from facĕre, 'to do, make').

diffondere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin diffŭndĕre ('to pour out in different directions, spread abroad, diffuse'), compound of dis- ('apart, abroad') + fŭndĕre ('to pour, melt').

dignità.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin dignĭtās, dignĭtātem ('worthiness, merit, honorable rank, dignity'), derived from dignus ('worthy, deserving').

dimenticare.etymology: Continues Late Latin dēmenticāre ('to lose one's mind, forget'), derived from Classical Latin dēmēns, dēmentis ('out of one's mind', from dē- + mēns, mentis, 'mind, memory'), displacing Classical oblīvīscī in Italian.

history.meaning: to let slip from the mind, forget

dipingere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dēpingĕre ('to paint thoroughly, depict, portray'), compound of dē- (intensive) + pingĕre ('to paint, embroider').

dipinto.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *dēpinctus (remodeled with the nasal infix of the present stem pingĕre) for Classical Latin dēpictus ('painted, depicted'); used both as the past participle/adjective 'painted' and as a masculine noun 'painting, picture'.

dire.etymology: Continues shortened Late Latin dīre for classical dīcere ('to say, tell'), keeping the dic- stem in dico, dici, dice, diciamo.

disastro.etymology: Formed in Renaissance Italian (whence French désastre and English disaster) from the pejorative prefix dis- ('ill, unfavorable') + astro ('star, planet, celestial influence', < Latin astrum < Greek ἄστρον, ástron), originally an astrological term meaning 'born under an unfavorable star'.

discorso.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical/Late Latin discŭrsus ('a running to and fro; in Late Latin, conversation, treatise, speech'), derived from discŭrrĕre ('to run about; to treat of a subject').

history.meaning: to run about -> Late Latin: conversation, discourse

discrezione.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin discrētiō, discrētiōnem ('separation; discernment, prudence, moderation'), derived from Classical Latin discernĕre ('to separate, distinguish, discern', past participle discrētus).

disegnare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dēsignāre ('to mark out, trace, outline, designate'), compound of dē- + signāre ('to mark', from signum, 'mark, sign').

disegno.etymology: Deverbal noun from disegnare ('to draw, outline, plan', < Classical Latin dēsignāre); exported from Renaissance Italian art theory to Europe (French dessin, English design).

history.meaning: to draw -> drawing, sketch, pattern, design

dispiacere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *displacēre (for Classical Latin displicēre, recomposed with the unreduced vowel of placēre, 'to please'), meaning 'to displease, cause regret or sorrow'.

history.meaning: to displease, be sorry, regret; sorrow (noun)

distanza.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin distantia ('standing apart, remoteness, distance, interval'), derived from distāns, present participle of distāre ('to stand apart, be distant', from dis- + stāre).

disturbare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin distŭrbāre ('to drive asunder, throw into disorder, disrupt, trouble'), compound of dis- + tŭrbāre ('to stir up, agitate', from tŭrba, 'crowd, commotion').

history.meaning: to throw into disorder, disrupt, trouble

disturbo.etymology: Deverbal noun from disturbare ('to disturb, bother', < Classical Latin distŭrbāre), meaning 'trouble, inconvenience, bother, ailment'.

dito.etymology: Continues Latin dĭgĭtum ('finger, pointer'); the collective feminine plural le dita reflects the Late Latin neuter plural dĭgĭta for the fingers as a set.

diventare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *dēventāre, frequentative built on Classical Latin dēvenīre ('to come down to, reach a state, become', past participle dēventus).

dividere.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin dīvĭdĕre ('to force apart, part, share, divide').

do.etymology: Musical note name introduced in the 17th century (often attributed to the theorist Giovanni Battista Doni) to replace Guido of Arezzo's closed-syllable ut (the first syllable of Ut queant laxis) with an open, easily sung syllable (either from Dominus, 'Lord', or from Doni's own surname); homophonous with do ('I give', < Latin dō).

history.meaning: first note of the diatonic scale (C)

doccia.etymology: Deverbal noun from docciare ('to pour in a stream, gush through a pipe'), derived from Vulgar Latin *dŭctia ('water conduit, gutter, spout', from Classical Latin dūcĕre, past participle dŭctus, 'to lead, channel water').

documento.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin docŭmentum ('lesson, example, warning, proof, official record'), derived from docēre ('to teach, show, prove').

history.meaning: to teach, show -> proof, example, official record

dodici.etymology: Continues Classical Latin duŏdĕcim ('twelve', compound of duŏ 'two' + dĕcem 'ten'), with regular monophthongization/reduction of unstressed uo to o and final -i on analogy with other numerals.

dolce.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dŭlcis, dŭlcem ('sweet, pleasant, gentle'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o and palatalization of -c- before a front vowel.

domani.etymology: Continues Late Latin dē māne ('in the early morning'), shifting from 'early next morning' to 'tomorrow'.
