domenica.etymology: Continues Christian Late Latin (diēs) Domĭnĭca ('the Lord's day'), feminine adjective from Classical Latin domĭnĭcus ('belonging to the master/Lord', from domĭnus, 'master, lord'), which replaced pagan diēs Sōlis ('day of the Sun') across Romance.

donna.etymology: Continues Latin dŏmĭna ('mistress of the household, lady'), syncopated in Vulgar Latin to *domna with assimilation -mn- > -nn-.

dopo.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *dē pŏst ('from behind, after'), compound of Classical Latin dē ('from') + pŏst ('behind, after').

dopotutto.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase dopo tutto ('after all'), formed from dopo ('after', < *dē pŏst) + tutto ('all, everything', < Late Latin tōttus for tōtus).

doppio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dŭplus ('twofold, double'), with regular lowering of short ŭ to closed o and Tuscan gemination/palatalization of postvocalic -pl- to -ppi- (compare coppia < cōpŭla).

dorato.etymology: Participial adjective from dorare ('to gild, coat with gold'), which continues Late Latin dēaurāre (compound of dē- + aurum, 'gold'), with regular monophthongization of au to o.

dormire.etymology: Continues Latin dormīre ('to sleep') directly in both spelling and conjugation.

dove.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *dē ŭbĭ ('from where, where'), compound of Classical Latin dē ('from') + ŭbĭ ('where'), with regular lowering of short ŭ to o and spirantization of intervocalic -b- to -v-.

dovere.etymology: Continues Latin dēbēre ('to owe; to be bound to'), with labialization of unstressed pretonic e to o before v.

dozzina.etymology: Derived from dodici ('twelve', < Latin duŏdĕcim) via Old Italian dozzina / Provençal dotzena ('group of twelve').

dritto.etymology: Syncopated popular form of diritto, continuing Vulgar Latin *dīrēctus (for Classical Latin dīrēctus, 'laid straight, direct, right', past participle of dīrĭgĕre, 'to set straight').

due.etymology: Continues Classical Latin duŏ / feminine duae ('two'), from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁ ('two'), with generalization of the feminine plural ending -e to both genders in standard Tuscan.

duetto.etymology: Derived in 18th-century Italian musical terminology from duo ('musical composition for two performers', < Latin duŏ, 'two') + the diminutive suffix -etto; borrowed internationally as duet.

history.meaning: composition or performance for two voices or instruments

durante.etymology: Grammaticalized preposition from the present participle of durare ('to last, endure', < Classical Latin dūrāre), originally used in absolute participial constructions (such as durante la guerra, 'while the war lasts').

duro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin dūrus ('hard, firm, tough, stern, harsh'), from Proto-Indo-European *dweh₂-ro- ('long-lasting, firm').

e.etymology: Continues Latin et ('and'), losing final -t before consonants while preserving optional ed before vowels.

ecco.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *eccu(m), reduced from Classical Latin eccum ('here he is, behold!'), itself a colloquial fusion of ecce ('behold!') + eum / hunc.

history.meaning: here is, here are, there is

eco.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin ēchō ('reflected sound, echo'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ, 'sound, reverberation, echo', personified as the mountain nymph Echo).

edera.etymology: Continues Latin hĕdĕra ('ivy'), with regular loss of initial h- and preservation of open tonic /ɛ/.

edificio.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin aedifĭcium ('building, structure, edifice'), derived from aedifĭcāre ('to build', compound of aedēs 'hearth, temple, house' + facĕre 'to make').

edilizio.etymology: Learned derivative of Classical Latin aedīlĭcius ('pertaining to an aedile', the Roman magistrate in charge of public buildings and streets, from aedīlis < aedēs, 'building, house'), adapted in modern Italian to mean 'relating to construction and the building trade'.

history.meaning: building -> magistrate of public works -> relating to public works

elegante.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin ēlegāns, ēlegantem ('choosy, fastidious, tasteful, graceful'), an old participial formation related to ēlĭgĕre ('to pick out, choose carefully', from ex- + legĕre).

emergenza.etymology: Derived as a learned philosophical and scientific noun from emergere (< Classical Latin ēmergĕre, 'to rise out of water, come to light'); in the modern sense 'sudden crisis, emergency', reinforced in the 19th–20th centuries as a semantic calque of English emergency.

history.meaning: to rise up, come to the surface

entrambi.etymology: Univerbation of Old Italian intra ambi / in trambi ('between both, both together'), from Latin inter ambōs ('between both', compound of inter + ambō, 'both').

entrare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin intrāre ('to go into, enter, penetrate'), denominative verb derived from intrā / intrō ('inside, within'), with regular lowering of initial unstressed i- to e- before a nasal cluster.

entro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin intrō ('inward, within, inside'), with regular lowering of short Latin ĭ to closed e.

erba.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hĕrba ('grass, green stalks, herb, weed'), with regular loss of Latin initial h-.

errore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin error, errōrem ('wandering, straying; mistake, error, delusion'), derived from errāre ('to wander, go astray, err').

history.meaning: to wander, stray -> straying, mistake, error

esattamente.etymology: Adverb formed from the feminine adjective esatta ('exact, precise', < Classical Latin exactus) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente).

esatto.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin exactus ('driven out; weighed or measured accurately, precise, exact'), past participle of exĭgĕre ('to drive out, demand, measure out', from ex- + agĕre).

history.meaning: to measure out, complete -> accurate, precise

espresso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin expressus ('squeezed out, pressed out; clearly articulated, explicit'), past participle of exprĭmĕre ('to press out', from ex- + premĕre); substantivized for a special fast messenger/train (treno espresso) and in late 19th-century Italy for coffee brewed on the spot under steam/water pressure (caffè espresso).

history.meaning: to press out -> pressed out, distinct, express

essere.etymology: Continues Latin esse ('to be') via Vulgar Latin *essere, blending forms from Latin esse and sedēre/stāre (such as past participle stato from status).

estate.etymology: Continues Classical Latin aestās, aestātem ('summer, summer heat', from the root of aestus, 'burning heat, glow', < Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ-, 'to burn'), with regular monophthongization of initial ae- to e-.

esterno.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin externus ('outward, external, foreign'), derived from exter / extrā ('outside').

etichetta.etymology: Borrowed from French étiquette ('small paper ticket or label attached to a dossier; court protocol'), from Middle Dutch stikken ('to stick, pin').

euro.etymology: Adopted in December 1995 by the European Council in Madrid as the name of the single European currency, clipped from Europa ('Europe', < Latin Eurōpa < Ancient Greek Εὐρώπη, Eurṓpē).

fa.etymology: In temporal phrases (due ore fa, 'two hours ago'), grammaticalized from the third-person singular present indicative fa ('it makes', < Latin facit, from facĕre); as the fourth note of the musical scale (F), taken by Guido of Arezzo from the initial syllable of Famuli tuorum in the hymn Ut queant laxis.

history.meaning: it makes (elapsed time: 'it makes two hours')
fourth syllable of Guido's hexachord hymn

faccia.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *facia, reshaped as a first-declension feminine noun from Classical Latin fifth-declension faciēs ('form, appearance, countenance, face', related to facĕre, 'to make, fashion'), with regular Tuscan gemination and palatalization of -ci- before a vowel.

facile.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin facĭlis ('easy to do, ready, compliant'), derived from facĕre ('to do, make').

facilmente.etymology: Adverb formed from the adjective facile ('easy', < Classical Latin facĭlis) + the adverbial suffix -mente (< Latin ablative mente).

faggio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *fāgĕus, adjective from Classical Latin fāgus ('beech tree'), cognate with English beech and German Buche.

falegname.etymology: Verb-noun compound formed within Italian from fare ('to make, work', 3rd-person singular stem fa-) + legname ('timber, woodwork', < Late Latin lignāmen, from Classical lignum, 'wood'), literally 'works-timber'.

famiglia.etymology: Continues Latin familia ('household', from famulus), shifting from an entire household estate to close kin.

familiare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin familiāris ('belonging to a household or family, domestic, intimate, friendly'), derived from familia ('household, family').

history.meaning: household, family -> of the family, familiar, intimate

fantastico.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin phantastĭcus ('imaginary, visionary'), borrowed from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós, 'able to imagine or present to the mind', from φαντάζειν, phantázein, 'to make visible', built on φαίνειν, phaínein, 'to shine, show').

fare.etymology: Continues shortened Late Latin fare for classical facere ('to make, do'), retaining the fac- stem in forms such as faccio, facciamo, facevo, and fatto (< factum).

farmacia.etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, 'use or preparation of drugs and medicines'), derived from φάρμακον (phármakon, 'medicinal herb, drug, remedy, potion').

fastidio.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin fastīdium ('loathing, aversion, squeamishness, annoyance'), derived from fastus ('haughtiness, disdain') + taedium ('weariness, disgust').

favore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin favor, favōrem ('goodwill, partiality, support, applause'), derived from favēre ('to be favorable to, befriend, support').

felice.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fēlīx, fēlīcem ('fruitful, fertile; auspicious, lucky, happy'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *dʰeh₁(y)- ('to suckle, nourish, produce').

feltro.etymology: Early Germanic loanword into Late Latin (*filtrum, cognate with Old High German filz and English felt) denoting matted, unspun wool.

fermare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin firmāre ('to make firm, strengthen, secure, fasten'), denominative verb from firmus ('firm, steadfast, stable'); in Italian the sense evolved from 'to fix securely in place' to 'to stop, halt' (and 'to lock/fasten').

history.meaning: firm -> to make firm, fix in place

fermata.etymology: Substantivized feminine past participle of fermare ('to stop, halt', < Classical Latin firmāre), designating a stopping place ('bus/tram stop'), a pause, or a musical hold sign (fermata).

history.meaning: to stop -> stop (bus/train stop), pause, musical fermata

fermo.etymology: Continues Latin firmus ('steady, solid, resolute'), keeping both physical ('still, motionless') and figurative ('firm') meanings.

ferramenta.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ferrāmenta ('iron implements, tools', neuter plural of ferrāmentum, derived from ferrum, 'iron'), reanalyzed in Italian as a feminine singular collective noun meaning 'ironmongery, hardware, hardware store'.

ferro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fĕrrum ('iron; any iron tool, weapon, or implement').

history.meaning: iron, iron tool (e.g., flatiron, knitting needle)

fessura.etymology: Continues Latin fissūra ('cleft, narrow chink, crack'), from fissus, past participle of findĕre ('to split, cleave').

festeggiare.etymology: Denominative verb formed within Italian from festa ('feast, holiday, celebration', < Late Latin festa, neuter plural of festum < Classical fēstus, 'festive, joyful') + the verbal suffix -eggiare.

fetta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *offītta, diminutive formed from Classical Latin offa ('bite-sized piece, morsel, lump of dough or meat') crossed with vitta ('band, ribbon, strip').

fiamma.etymology: Continues Classical Latin flamma ('blazing fire, flame', from *flagma, related to flagrāre, 'to blaze, burn'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial fl- to fi- (/fj/).

fiancata.etymology: Derived within Italian from fianco ('side, flank, hip', borrowed via Old French flanc from Frankish *hlanka, 'hip, side') + the suffix -ata, designating the side wall of a building, ship, or vehicle.

history.meaning: flank, side -> side panel, side of a vehicle or building

fianco.etymology: Entered Romance via Frankish *hlanka ('hip, flank, bend of the body'), via Old French flanc with regular Italian outcomes fl- > fi-.

fiato.etymology: Continues Classical Latin flātus, flātum ('a blowing, breathing, breath, breeze', derived from flāre, 'to blow, breathe'), with regular Tuscan evolution of initial fl- to fi- (/fj/).

history.meaning: to blow, breathe -> breath, puff of wind

fiero.etymology: Continues Latin fĕrus ('untamed, spirited, bold'), whose chivalric sense shifted via Old French fier toward 'noble, proud'.

fila.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin fīla ('threads, row, line'), originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin fīlum ('thread, string, contour'), reanalyzed as a feminine singular collective noun meaning 'line, row, queue'.

filetto.etymology: Diminutive of filo ('thread, line, edge', < Classical Latin fīlum) formed with -etto (reinforced in culinary usage by French filet), designating a narrow decorative line, screw thread, or tenderloin fillet.

history.meaning: fine thread, screw thread, narrow stripe, fillet of meat/fish

filo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fīlum ('thread, yarn, cord, filament, edge of a blade').

history.meaning: thread, wire, string, blade edge, bit

finale.etymology: Continues Late Latin fīnālis ('pertaining to the end, final'), derived from Classical Latin fīnis ('boundary, limit, end').

finché.etymology: Univerbation of the conjunctional phrase fin che (or fino a che, 'until, as long as'), from fino ('up to, until', < Latin fīnis) + che ('that', < Latin quid / quod).

fine.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fīnis, fīnem ('boundary, border, limit, end, purpose'); as an adjective ('thin, refined, fine'), derived in Vulgar Latin (*fīnus) from fīnīre ('to finish, bring to perfection').

finestra.etymology: Continues Latin fenestra ('window, opening for light'), with raising of unstressed e to i in the initial syllable.

finire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fīnīre ('to bound, limit, bring to an end, finish'), denominative verb from fīnis ('limit, end').

history.meaning: end -> to bring to an end, finish

finissimo.etymology: Absolute superlative of fine / fino ('fine, thin, pure, choice', < Vulgar Latin *fīnus, derived from fīnis / fīnīre, 'perfected, finished to the highest degree') formed with -issimo.

finito.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fīnītus ('bounded, finished, completed, ended'), past participle of fīnīre ('to finish, bring to an end').

fino.etymology: As a preposition ('until, up to, as far as'), apheretic form of infino, from Latin in fīne ('at/to the limit or end', from fīnis); as an adjective ('thin, pure, fine'), from Vulgar Latin *fīnus ('finished, perfected').

history.meaning: to the limit, up to the end
until, up to, as far as (prep.); fine, thin (adj.)

fiore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin flōs, flōrem ('flower, blossom, prime, best part'), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃-s ('blossom'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial fl- to fi- (/fj/).

firma.etymology: Deverbal noun from firmare ('to sign, validate a document with one's signature', < Classical Latin firmāre, 'to make firm, ratify, confirm in writing').

history.meaning: to ratify by signing -> signature; designer label

fissare.etymology: Denominative verb from fisso ('fixed, fastened, steady', < Classical Latin fīxus, past participle of fīgĕre, 'to drive in, fasten, fix'), meaning 'to fix, fasten, set (a date/appointment), stare at'.

history.meaning: fixed -> to fix, fasten, arrange, stare at

fisso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fīxus ('driven in, fastened, immovable, fixed'), past participle of fīgĕre ('to drive in, fix, fasten'), with regular assimilation of -x- to -ss-.

fiume.etymology: Continues Classical Latin flūmen ('flowing water, stream, river', derived from fluĕre, 'to flow'), with regular Tuscan evolution of initial fl- to fi- (/fj/).

foglia.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fŏlia ('leaves'), neuter plural of fŏlium ('leaf', cognate with Ancient Greek φύλλον, phýllon), reanalyzed in Vulgar Latin as a feminine singular noun ('leaf of a plant').

foglio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fŏlium ('leaf of a plant; sheet of papyrus or parchment'), retaining the masculine gender of the Latin neuter singular to designate a 'sheet of paper, page'.

fondo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fŭndus ('bottom, lowest part, foundation; piece of land, estate'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

fontana.etymology: Continues Late Latin fontāna (originally feminine of the adjective fontānus, 'of a spring', with aqua 'water' understood, from Classical Latin fōns, fontis, 'spring, fountain').

formaggio.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century from Old French formage (modern French fromage), from Vulgar Latin *(cāseus) formāticus ('cheese made in a wicker mold or form', derived from Classical Latin forma, 'mold, form'), supplementing Tuscan cacio (< cāseus).

formale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin formālis ('relating to form, serving as a model, formal'), derived from forma ('shape, form, model').

fornaia.etymology: Continues Classical Latin furnāria (feminine of furnārius, 'baker', derived from furnus, 'oven'), with regular Tuscan evolution of the suffix -āria to -aia.

fornello.etymology: Diminutive in -ello of forno ('oven, furnace', < Latin fŭrnus), designating a small brazier or kitchen stove burner.

forno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fŭrnus ('oven, bakehouse'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

forse.etymology: Continues Classical Latin forsitan ('perhaps, maybe', itself a contraction of fors sit an, 'there may be a chance whether'), reduced in Vulgar Latin and Old Italian to forsi > forse.

history.meaning: it may be a chance whether -> perhaps

forte.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fŏrtis, fŏrtem ('strong, powerful, vigorous, brave, loud'), from Old Latin forctus.

fortuna.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fortūna ('chance, luck, fate, good fortune', personified as the goddess Fortuna), derived from fors, fortis ('chance, lot').

foto.etymology: Colloquial clipping (apocope) of fotografia ('photograph, photography'), internationally coined from Ancient Greek φῶς, φωτός (phôs, phōtós, 'light') + -γραφία (-graphía, 'drawing, writing').

fradicio.etymology: Metathesised Tuscan outcome (via *fracĭdus) of Latin fracĭdus ('overripe, sodden, softened by moisture'), from fracēre.

fragola.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *fragŭla, diminutive of Classical Latin frāga ('wild strawberries', neuter plural of frāgum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular collective noun).

francese.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *francēnsis (from Late Latin Francus, 'Frank', + ethnonymic suffix -ēnsis, with regular reduction of -ns- to -s-), replacing older Tuscan francesco.

frase.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis ('diction, style of expression, phrase'), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, 'speech, way of speaking, expression', derived from φράζειν, phrázein, 'to point out, declare, tell').

fratellino.etymology: Diminutive of fratello ('brother', itself originally a diminutive < Vulgar Latin *frātellus from Classical Latin frāter, 'brother') formed with the affectionate suffix -ino.

fratello.etymology: Continues Latin frātellum, originally an affectionate diminutive of frāter ('brother') that replaced bare frate in everyday kinship.

freccia.etymology: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from Old French fleche ('arrow', of Frankish origin, cf. *fliugika, 'flying shaft', related to *fleuganą, 'to fly', or *flikka), with dissimilation of fl- to fr-.

freddo.etymology: Continues syncopated Vulgar Latin *frigdu(m) for classical frīgidus ('cold'), with assimilation of -gd- > -dd-.

fresco.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Germanic (Lombardic or Frankish) *frisk ('fresh, cool, newly made, vigorous', from Proto-Germanic *friskaz), whence also the art term affresco ('painted on fresh wet plaster').

fretta.etymology: Deverbal noun from frettare ('to rub vigorously, scrub, hasten'), continuing Vulgar Latin *frictāre, frequentative of Classical Latin fricāre ('to rub, chafe', past participle frictus), shifting from 'brisk rubbing' to 'haste, hurry'.

frigo.etymology: Colloquial clipping (apocope) of frigorifero ('refrigerator'), a learned compound from Classical Latin frīgus, frīgŏris ('cold') + -fer ('bearing, producing', from ferre).

frizzante.etymology: Participial adjective from frizzare ('to sting, tingle, sparkle, effervesce'), either from Vulgar Latin *frīctiāre (derived from frīgĕre, 'to fry, sizzle', past participle frīctus) or of expressive origin imitating a sizzling/fizzing sensation.

history.meaning: to fizz, sparkle -> sparkling, fizzy, lively

fronte.etymology: Continues Classical Latin frōns, frontem ('forehead, brow; forepart, front, facade').

funzionare.etymology: Denominative verb formed from funzione ('function, performance, operation', learned borrowing from Classical Latin functiō, functiōnem, from fungī, 'to perform, execute'), modeled in the 19th century on French fonctionner.

fuori.etymology: Continues Classical Latin fŏrīs ('out of doors, outside, abroad', originally the ablative/locative plural of fŏris, 'door, double door'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ŏ to uo.

furbo.etymology: Originally Renaissance jargon furbo ('pickpocket, streetwise rogue', via French fourbe linked to fourbir, 'to polish/clean out'), later softened to 'clever, smart'.

furgone.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th–19th century from French fourgon ('baggage wagon, delivery van'), of uncertain origin (Connected either with Old French fourgon, 'oven poker', < Late Latin furcōnem from furca, 'fork', or with Germanic words for wagon).

fusibile.etymology: Derived from Late Latin fūsĭbĭlis ('capable of being melted, molten', from Classical Latin fundĕre, past participle fūsus, 'to melt, pour'); substantivized in electrical engineering for a safety 'fuse' that melts when current is excessive.

gamba.etymology: Continues Late Latin gamba / camba ('hock or pastern joint of a quadruped, leg', attested in 4th-century veterinary treatises), borrowed from Ancient Greek καμπή (kampḗ, 'bend, curve, limb joint'), which in Italian and French (jambe) displaced Classical Latin crūs.

gancio.etymology: Borrowed in the 15th–16th century through Mediterranean maritime trade from Spanish/Catalan gancho ('hook, boat hook') or Turkish kanca / Modern Greek γάντζος (gántzos), ultimately linked to a pre-Roman/Celtic root *ganskio- ('branch, fork, hook').

gara.etymology: Attested in Tuscan since the 14th century (originally in the phrase a gara, 'in rivalry, vying with one another'), probably borrowed from Old French gare / garer or Germanic *warōn ('to watch out, contend, strive') or Arabic غَارَة (ġāra, 'raid, horse-race, charge').

history.meaning: in emulation, vying -> contest, competition, race

gemello.etymology: Continues Classical Latin gemĕllus ('twin-born, twin, double'), diminutive of gemĭnus ('twin').

generoso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin generōsus ('of noble birth, high-born; magnanimous, noble-minded, generous'), derived from genus, genĕris ('birth, lineage, stock').

gentile.etymology: Continues Classical Latin gentīlis ('belonging to the same clan or gens', from gēns, gentis), which in medieval Romance (reinforced by Old Occitan and Old French gentil) evolved to mean 'of noble birth, courteous, refined, kind'.

history.meaning: clan, family -> belonging to a noble clan

gesso.etymology: Continues Latin gy̆psum ('gypsum, plaster, chalk'), borrowed from Greek γύψος (gýpsos), with regular assimilation of -ps- > -ss-.

ghiacciato.etymology: Participial adjective from ghiacciare ('to freeze, turn to ice'), derived from ghiaccio ('ice', < Vulgar Latin *glacia for Classical glaciēs, 'ice').

history.meaning: ice -> to freeze -> iced, ice-cold, frozen

ghiaccio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *glăcĭum (masculine reshaping of Classical feminine glăcĭēs, 'ice'), with regular outcome gl- > ghi- and -cj- > -cci-.

giacca.etymology: Borrowed via French jaque ('short close-fitting tunic or padded coat') from Middle French Jacque (the nickname 'Jack' applied to French peasants, Jacques Bonhomme, who wore such short tunics).

history.meaning: short peasant tunic or padded jerkin

giallo.etymology: Borrowed in the Middle Ages from Old French jalne (modern French jaune), which continues Classical Latin galbĭnus ('greenish-yellow, chartreuse', derived from galbus, 'yellow').

history.meaning: yellow; mystery/thriller fiction (from the 1929 Mondadori yellow covers)

giardino.etymology: Borrowed from Old French jardin ('garden'), itself from Frankish *gardo ('enclosure, yard').

gioia.etymology: Borrowed in the 13th century (through Sicilian and Tuscan courtly poetry) from Old French joie ('joy, delight; jewel'), which continues Late/Vulgar Latin gaudia (neuter plural of Classical Latin gaudium, 'joy, gladness', reanalyzed as a feminine singular noun).

giornale.etymology: Substantivised use of the adjective giornale (< Latin diurnālis, 'daily', from diēs, 'day'), originally foglio giornale ('daily sheet').

giornata.etymology: Derived from giorno ('day', < Late Latin diurnum) + the suffix -ata (paralleling Old French jornee and Old Occitan jornada), designating the whole span, weather, or work of a day.

giorno.etymology: Continues Late/Vulgar Latin diŭrnum (substantivized neuter of Classical Latin diŭrnus, 'of the day, daily', derived from diēs, 'day'), with regular palatalization of initial di- to gi- (/dʒ/).

giovane.etymology: Continues Classical Latin iŭvĕnis, iŭvĕnem ('young, youthful; a young person'), with regular palatalization of Latin initial consonantal i- to gi- (/dʒ/) and lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

giovedì.etymology: Continues Latin Iŏvis diēs ('Jove's day, day of Jupiter'), fused into a single oxytone compound like lunedì through venerdì.

girare.etymology: Continues Late Latin gȳrāre ('to turn around in a circle, revolve, wheel'), denominative verb from Classical Latin gȳrus ('circle, circular course, ring', borrowed from Ancient Greek γῦρος, gŷros).

history.meaning: to turn in a circle, rotate
to turn, spin, tour, stir, film

girella.etymology: Diminutive derived from giro ('turn, circle, wheel') or girare ('to turn, spin') with the suffix -ella, designating a small pulley wheel, swivel, or spiral-rolled pastry/sweet.

history.meaning: small wheel, pulley, pinwheel, spiral roll

giro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin gȳrus ('circle, circular course, turn, ring'), borrowed from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gŷros, 'ring, circle'), or deverbal from girare.

giunto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin iūnctus ('joined, yoked, united, arrived'), past participle of iŭngĕre ('to join, yoke, connect'); as a noun, designates a mechanical joint, coupling, or seam.

giusto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin iūstus ('upright, righteous, lawful, exact, right'), derived from iūs ('law, right'), with regular palatalization of initial consonantal i- to gi- (/dʒ/).

già.etymology: Continues Classical Latin iam ('already, now, by this time'), with regular palatalization of initial consonantal i- to gi- (/dʒ/), loss of final -m, and syntactic gemination of a following consonant.

giù.etymology: Apocopated form of Old Italian giuso ('down, downward, below'), which continues Late Latin iūsum (attested variant of Classical Latin deōrsum, 'downward', remodeled with initial i- on analogy with its antonym sūsum < sūrsum, 'upward').

glassa.etymology: Borrowed from French glace ('ice; sugar icing, glaze', from Vulgar Latin *glacia < Classical glaciēs, 'ice') or back-formed from glassare (< French glacer, 'to glaze, coat with icing').

gli.etymology: Continues Classical Latin illī: as the masculine plural definite article ('the', before vowels, s + consonant, z, gn, ps), from nominative plural illī via Old Italian li; as the third-person dative clitic pronoun ('to him, to them'), from dative singular illī.

history.form: illī (nom. pl. and dat. sg. of ille)

history.meaning: the (masc. pl.); to him, to them

goccia.etymology: Deverbal noun from gocciare ('to drip, drop'), which continues Vulgar Latin *gŭttiāre, derived from Classical Latin gŭtta ('drop of liquid').

goccio.etymology: Masculine variant of goccia ('drop', from gocciare < Vulgar Latin *gŭttiāre, built on Classical Latin gŭtta, 'drop'), specialized in everyday Italian for a small sip, dash, or splash of a beverage (un goccio d'acqua / di vino).

history.meaning: drop -> small splash, sip, dash of liquid

gocciolare.etymology: Frequentative/diminutive verb formed within Italian from gocciare ('to drip', < Vulgar Latin *gŭttiāre) or from gocciola ('droplet', diminutive of goccia) + -are, meaning 'to drip, trickle'.

gomma.etymology: Continues Late Latin gŭmma (reshaped as a first-declension feminine from Classical Latin indeclinable cŭmmĭ / gŭmmĭ, 'plant resin, gum'), borrowed via Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi) from Egyptian kmyt ('gum, resin').

gonfiare.etymology: Continues Classical Latinare-compound cōnflāre ('to blow together, blow up, inflate, kindle'), compound of com- + flāre ('to blow'), with voicing of initial c- to g- and regular Tuscan evolution of -fl- to -fi-.

gonfio.etymology: Syncopated participial adjective (for gonfiato) or deverbal adjective from gonfiare ('to inflate, swell', < Classical Latin cōnflāre), meaning 'swollen, puffed up, inflated'.

gradino.etymology: Diminutive of grado ('step, stair, degree', < Classical Latin grădus, 'step, pace, stair, rank') formed with the suffix -ino, designating an individual stair step or rung.

grande.etymology: Continues Classical Latin grandis, grandem ('full-grown, large, great, grand'), which across Vulgar Latin and Romance largely displaced magnus ('great, large').

graticcio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *crātīcius (from Classical Latin crātīcius, 'made of wickerwork or hurdles', derived from crātis, 'wickerwork, lattice, hurdle'), with voicing of initial cr- to gr-.

history.meaning: wicker hurdle, lattice -> made of latticework

gratis.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin grātīs (contracted from grātiīs, ablative plural of grātia, 'favor, kindness, thanks'), literally 'out of kindness, for thanks alone, without payment'.

history.meaning: favor, thanks -> for nothing, without pay

grazie.etymology: Plural of grazia, from Latin grātia ('favour, goodwill, thanks'), shortened from phrases like tante grazie / rendo grazie ('I render thanks').

gres.etymology: Borrowed from French grès ('sandstone; vitrified stoneware ceramic'), which derives from Frankish *griōt ('gravel, coarse sand, grit', cognate with Old High German grioz and English grit).

gridare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *crītāre, a popular phonetic reduction of Classical Latin quirītāre ('to raise a plaintive cry, shriek, call upon the Quirites [Roman citizens] for help'), with voicing of initial cr- to gr-.

history.meaning: to cry out for citizen aid, scream

grigio.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Germanic (Frankish or Lombardic) *grīs ('gray', from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz) via Medieval Latin grīseus, with regular Tuscan palatalization of -si- to -gi- (/ʒ/ > /dʒ/).

griglia.etymology: Borrowed in the 17th–18th century from French grille ('iron grating, gridiron, grill'), which continues Late Latin crāticŭla ('small hurdle, gridiron', diminutive of Classical Latin crātis, 'wickerwork, lattice').

grosso.etymology: Continues Late Latin grŏssus ('thick, coarse, bulky, big'), a colloquial word that arose in Imperial/Late Latin to express thickness and bulk alongside grandis.

guardare.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Germanic (Frankish or Lombardic) *wardōn ('to watch over, guard, look out for, direct one's eyes toward', from Proto-Germanic *wardōną), with regular adaptation of Germanic initial w- as gu-.

guida.etymology: Deverbal noun from guidare ('to guide, lead, drive'), which derives from Germanic (Gothic or Lombardic) *wītan / Frankish *wītan ('to show the way, direct, watch over', from Proto-Germanic *wītaną, 'to look after, know').

guscio.etymology: Probably continues Vulgar Latin *cŭscĭum / Greek κυστίον (kystíon, 'little bladder, pod, husk'), with sonorisation of initial k- > g-.

gustare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin gŭstāre ('to taste, take a little of, enjoy'), built on the stem of gŭstus ('taste, sipping').

i.etymology: Masculine plural definite article ('the', used before single consonants other than s+consonant, z, gn, ps), reduced in Old Italian from li (< Classical Latin nominative plural illī, 'those').

idea.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical/Late Latin idĕa ('Platonic form, archetype, concept'), from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, 'look, semblance, form, ideal prototype', derived from ἰδεῖν, ideîn, 'to see').

history.meaning: appearance, form, ideal pattern (from ideîn, 'to see')

ideale.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin idĕālis ('existing in idea or archetype, archetypal'), derived from idĕa (< Ancient Greek ἰδέα, idéa).

identico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval/Scholastic Latin identĭcus ('the very same, identical'), derived from Late Latin identĭtās ('sameness', coined from Classical Latin īdem, 'the same').

ieri.etymology: Continues Latin herī ('yesterday'), with regular diphthongization of stressed open e to ie (/ˈjɛri/).

il.etymology: Masculine singular definite article ('the'), developed in Old Italian by apheresis from unstressed accusative illum ('that', > lo / 'l > il, with prosthetic vowel support before a single consonant).

imbattibile.etymology: Adjective formed within Italian from negative prefix in- (assimilated to im- before labial b) + battibile ('beatable', from battere, 'to beat, defeat', + -bile), meaning 'unbeatable'.

immobile.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin immōbĭlis ('unmovable, motionless, steadfast'), negative compound of in- ('not') + mōbĭlis ('movable', from movēre, 'to move'); substantivized in law and commerce (bene immobile) for 'real estate, building'.

immobiliare.etymology: Derived from immobile ('real-estate property, building', < Classical Latin immōbĭlis, as in res immobiles) + the relational suffix -are (modeled on French immobilier), meaning 'real-estate, property-related'.

impacchettare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed within Italian from in- (assimilated to im- before p) + pacchetto ('packet, small package, parcel', diminutive of pacco) + -are, meaning 'to wrap up, package'.

imparare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *imparāre (in- + parāre, 'to acquire, prepare for oneself, store in the mind').

impastare.etymology: Prefixed verb formed in Late/Medieval Latin (impastāre) from in- + pasta ('dough, paste', < Greek πάστη).

impasto.etymology: Deverbal noun from impastare ('to knead, mix into dough or paste'), parasynthetic verb formed from in- ('into') + pasta ('dough, paste', < Late Latin pasta < Ancient Greek πάστη, pástē, 'barley porridge, salted mess').

history.meaning: to knead, mix -> dough, batter, mixture

impeccabile.etymology: Learned continuation of Christian Late Latin impeccābĭlis ('incapable of sinning, sinless, faultless'), negative compound of in- ('not') + peccābĭlis (from peccāre, 'to sin, err, make a mistake').

impiegato.etymology: Substantivized past participle of impiegare ('to employ, engage in a post or task', < Classical Latin implicāre, 'to enfold, entwine, engage, involve', via Old Italian/French influence), designating a salaried office worker or clerk.

history.meaning: to employ -> employee, office worker, clerk

importante.etymology: Participial adjective from the present participle of importare ('to bring in; to matter, be of consequence', < Classical Latin importāre, 'to carry in, introduce, entail').

history.meaning: to matter, be of consequence -> important, significant

in.etymology: Continues Latin in ('in, into, on'), expressing spatial enclosure, country/region location, transport (in treno), and states.

incastrato.etymology: Participial adjective from incastrare ('to fit into a groove, mortise, wedge, jam'), which continues Medieval/Vulgar Latin *incastrāre (from in- + castrum or borrowing from Ancient Greek γάστρα / *ἐγκάστριον, 'notch, socket, joint').

history.meaning: to set into a slot or bezel, mortise
to fit tightly, wedge -> wedged, stuck, jammed

inchiostro.etymology: Continues Late Latin encaustum ('purple-red imperial ink burned or fixed with heat', borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔγκαυστον, énkauston, neuter of ἔγκαυστος, 'burned in', from ἐν + καίειν, 'to burn'), reshaped in Vulgar Latin as *enclaustrum by folk-etymological crossing with claustrum.

incidere.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin incīdĕre ('to cut into, carve, engrave, incise', from in- + caedĕre, 'to cut, strike'), and in the intransitive sense ('to impinge, have an impact') from Classical Latin incĭdĕre (from in- + cadĕre, 'to fall upon').

history.meaning: to cut into, engrave / to fall upon, affect
to engrave, carve, record; to affect, have an impact

inclinare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin inclīnāre ('to cause to lean, bend, tilt, incline'), compound of in- ('toward') + *clīnāre ('to lean, slope', cognate with Greek κλίνειν, klínein).

includere.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin inclūdĕre ('to shut in, enclose, include'), compound of in- ('in') + claudĕre ('to shut, close').

incluso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin inclūsus ('shut in, enclosed, included'), past participle of inclūdĕre (from in- + claudĕre, 'to shut').

incompiuto.etymology: Adjective formed within Italian from the negative prefix in- ('not') + compiuto ('completed, finished, accomplished', past participle of compiere < Vulgar Latin *complīre for Classical complēre, 'to fill up, complete').

incontrare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed in Vulgar Latin or early Italian from in- ('in, toward') + contra ('against, opposite, facing', < Classical Latin contrā), meaning 'to come face to face with, meet'.

incontro.etymology: Deverbal noun from incontrare ('to meet', from in + contra), used both as a masculine noun ('meeting, encounter, match') and adverbially/prepositionally (andare incontro a, 'to go to meet').

history.meaning: to meet, come face to face

indelebile.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin indēlēbĭlis ('imperishable, that cannot be erased or blotted out'), negative compound of in- ('not') + dēlēbĭlis ('erasable', from dēlēre, 'to erase, wipe out, destroy').

history.meaning: not + to erase -> unable to be erased, indelible

indicare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin indĭcāre ('to point out, make known, disclose, indicate'), denominative verb from index, indĭcis ('pointer, forefinger, informer').

history.meaning: pointer -> to point out, show, indicate
to point at, point out, indicate

indietro.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase in dietro ('in back, backward'), from in (< Latin in) + dietro ('behind', < Vulgar Latin dē rĕtrō).

indirizzo.etymology: Deverbal noun from indirizzare ('to direct, guide, address'), parasynthetic verb formed from in- + dirizzare ('to set straight, direct', < Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre, built on Classical Latin dīrēctus, 'straight, direct').

history.meaning: to direct, address -> direction, street/mailing address

indossare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from in- ('on, upon') + dosso ('back, shoulders', < Vulgar Latin dŏssum, with assimilation of -rs- to -ss- from Classical Latin dŏrsum, 'back'), literally 'to put on one's back'.

history.meaning: on one's back -> to put on, wear (clothing)

indovinare.etymology: Derived from Old Italian indovino ('soothsayer, diviner, fortune-teller', < Classical Latin dīvīnus, 'prophetic, soothsayer', with prefixation of in- on analogy with inspirare / incantare), meaning 'to divine, foretell, guess rightly'.

infilare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from in- ('into, onto') + filo ('thread, line', < Classical Latin fīlum) + -are, originally 'to pass a thread through the eye of a needle or beads onto a string', then generalized to 'to slip on (clothes), slide or insert into'.

history.meaning: to thread, slip on, insert into

infornare.etymology: Parasynthetic verb formed from in- ('into') + forno ('oven', < Classical Latin fŭrnus) + -are (attested in Late Latin as infurnāre), meaning 'to put into the oven, bake'.

history.meaning: oven -> to put into the oven
to put in the oven, bake

inglese.etymology: Continues Vulgar/Medieval Latin Anglēnsis ('English, of the Angles', from Late Latin Anglī, 'the Angles', a Germanic people of Britain, + suffix -ēnsis), with palatal dissimilation/influence of Old French engleis yielding initial in-.

ingresso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin ingrĕssus ('a going into, entering, entrance, beginning'), action noun derived from ingrĕdī ('to step into, enter', from in- + grădī, 'to step, walk').

history.meaning: to step in, enter -> entrance, entry

iniziale.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin inĭtĭālis ('pertaining to the beginning, initial'), derived from Classical Latin inĭtĭum ('entrance, beginning'); substantivized in the feminine (lettera iniziale) for the first letter of a word or name.

iniziare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin inĭtĭāre ('to begin, originate; to initiate into sacred mysteries'), denominative verb derived from inĭtĭum ('beginning').

inizio.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin inĭtĭum ('a going in, entrance, beginning, origin'), derived from inīre ('to go into, enter upon, begin', compound of in- + īre, 'to go').

insaponato.etymology: Participial adjective from insaponare ('to lather or rub with soap'), parasynthetic verb formed from in- + sapone ('soap', < Classical Latin sāpō, sāpōnem, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ).

history.meaning: to soap, lather -> soaped, soapy, lathered

insegna.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin insĭgnia ('badges, standards, emblems'), originally the neuter plural of Classical Latin insĭgne ('distinguishing mark, badge, standard', from in- + signum, 'mark, sign'), reanalyzed as a feminine singular noun meaning 'banner, shop sign, emblem'.

insegnare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *insĭgnāre ('to mark out, point out, show by signs, instruct'), compound of in- + Classical Latin signāre ('to mark, designate', from signum, 'sign, mark'), which across Romance largely replaced Classical docēre ('to teach').

history.meaning: to mark -> to point out, instruct

insieme.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *insĕmel ('at the same time, together'), reinforced compound of Classical Latin in + sĕmel ('once, a single time, simultaneously'), with Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ĕ to ie.

history.meaning: once, at the same time -> together

intero.etymology: Continues Classical Latin intĕger, intĕgrum ('untouched, whole, complete, intact', from in- 'not' + root of tangĕre 'to touch'), via Vulgar Latin paroxytonic *intĕgru with vocalization/reduction of the intervocalic -gr- cluster (likely reinforced by Old Occitan entier / Old French entier).

interruttore.etymology: Learned agent/instrument noun from Late Latin interrŭptor, interrŭptōrem ('one who breaks off or interrupts', from Classical Latin interrŭmpĕre, 'to break apart, interrupt', past participle interrŭptus); specialized in electrical engineering for an electrical 'switch' or circuit breaker.

intorno.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase in torno ('in a circle, around'), from in + torno ('turn, lathe, circular movement', deverbal from tornare < Latin tornāre, 'to turn on a lathe, round off').

history.meaning: to turn on a lathe, round

inumidirsi.etymology: Reflexive form of inumidire ('to moisten, dampen'), parasynthetic verb formed from in- + umido ('damp, moist, humid', learned continuation of Classical Latin ūmĭdus / hūmĭdus, from ūmēre, 'to be moist') + -ire.

history.meaning: to moisten -> to become damp or moist

invece.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase in vece ('in place [of], instead'), continuing Classical Latin in vĭcem ('in turn, in place of', accusative/ablative vĭce of defective *vĭx, 'change, alternation, stead').

history.meaning: instead, on the other hand, whereas

inverno.etymology: Continues Late/Vulgar Latin hībernum (substantivized neuter from Classical Latin tempus hībernum, 'wintry season, winter', derived from hiĕms, 'winter'), with insertion of epenthetic -n- in the initial syllable (*imbĕrnum / *invĕrnum).

lampo.etymology: Deverbal noun from Old Italian lampare ('to flash, gleam'), continuing Late Latin lampāre from Greek λάμπειν (lámpein, 'to shine').

latte.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *lactem (for classical neuter lac, stem lact-, 'milk'), with assimilation of -ct- > -tt- and masculine gender in Italian.

lavagna.etymology: Named after Lavagna on the Ligurian coast near Genoa, historic quarry center for the dark splitting slate used in school boards and roofs.

leggio.etymology: Derived from leggere ('to read', < Latin lĕgĕre) with the instrument/place suffix -ìo, denoting a slanted stand for holding books or sheet music.

lente.etymology: Continues Latin lēns, lĕntem ('lentil'), transferred in 13th-century Italian optics to convex glass discs shaped like a lentil seed.

lenticchia.etymology: Continues Latin lentĭcŭla ('little lentil'), diminutive of lēns, lĕntis ('lentil', source also of lente, 'glass lens').

lettera.etymology: Continues Latin littera ('alphabetic character'; plural litterae, 'written epistle, letter'), uniting both meanings in singular Italian lettera.

limone.etymology: Entered medieval Italian through Mediterranean trade from Arabic laymūn and Persian līmūn.

lo.etymology: Develops from Latin illum, accusative masculine singular of the demonstrative ille ('that'), losing its initial syllable in unstressed proclitic position.

locanda.etymology: From the Latin gerundive phrase (domus) locanda, '(a house) to be let/rented out', from locāre ('to place, rent out')—originally written on signs outside inns.

lunedì.etymology: Continues Latin lūnae diēs ('day of the Moon'), fusing the genitive lūnae with dì (< diēs).

mandorla.etymology: Continues Late Latin amandŭla (alteration of Classical amygdăla, from Greek ἀμυγδάλη, amygdálē, 'almond'), with apheresis of initial a-.

mangiare.etymology: Borrowed via Old French mangier from Spoken Latin mandūcāre ('to chew, eat heartily'), which replaced classical edere.

manica.etymology: Continues Latin manĭca ('long tunic sleeve covering the hand'), derived from mănus ('hand').

manico.etymology: Continues Late Latin *manĭcus ('handle, grip'), built on Latin mănus ('hand'), literally 'the part held in the hand'.

mansarda.etymology: Borrowed from French mansarde, named after the seventeenth-century French architect François Mansart, who popularized habitable rooms beneath pitched roofs.

mattina.etymology: Substantivized feminine of Latin mātūtīna (hōra), '(hour) of Matuta', the Roman goddess of the dawn.

melodia.etymology: Continues Late Latin melōdĭa, from Greek μελῳδία (melōidía, 'singing, choral song'), compound of μέλος (mélos, 'musical phrase') + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, 'song').

mescolare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *misculāre, frequentative/diminutive derivative of Classical Latin miscēre ('to mix, mingle').

messaggio.etymology: Borrowed via Old Provençal messatge / Old French message from Vulgar Latin *missātĭcum ('that which is sent'), from Latin mĭttĕre ('to send').

mezzanotte.etymology: Univerbation of mezza notte, continuing Latin mĕdĭa nŏx / mĕdĭam nŏctem ('middle of the night').

mezzogiorno.etymology: Transparent compound of mezzo ('half, middle', from Latin medius) + giorno ('day'), naming twelve noon (and, by extension, southern Italy where the midday sun stands).

miele.etymology: Continues Latin mel, stem mell- ('honey'), diphthongizing stressed open e to ie in open syllable.

moneta.etymology: Continues Latin monēta ('mint; coin'), from the temple of Iūnō Monēta on Rome's Capitoline Hill where silver coins were struck.

montagna.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *montānĕa (neuter plural of montānĕus, 'of mountains', treated as a feminine singular collective), derived from Latin mōns, mŏntis.

muscolo.etymology: Learned/semi-learned continuation of Latin mūscŭlus ('little mouse; muscle', comparing the rippling of a flexed biceps under the skin to a mouse).

neve.etymology: Continues Latin nĭx, nĭvem ('snow'), from the accusative nĭvem with regular Romance development ĭ > closed /e/.

niente.etymology: Exact Latin source debated; Treccani notes several proposals—most prominently Vulgar Latin *nec gentem ('not a soul/person') or *ne inde—with medieval Tuscan variants neente and neiente.

no.etymology: Continues Latin nōn in stressed standalone position, whereas unstressed proclitic position before a verb preserved the final nasal as non.

non.etymology: Continues Latin nōn (itself from Old Latin noenum, 'not one'). In Italian it stands directly before the verb phrase to negate a clause.

nonna.etymology: Continues Late Latin nŏnna ('revered elder woman, nun, grandmother'), an affectionate nursery reduplication.

nonno.etymology: Continues Late Latin nonnus (originally a respectful address to an elder or monk), which replaced classical avus as the everyday word for grandfather.

occhiale.etymology: Derived from occhio ('eye', < Latin oculus); plural gli occhiali ('eyeglasses') was coined in late-thirteenth-century Italy where wearable spectacles were first crafted.

odore.etymology: Continues Latin odōr, odōrem ('smell, scent, fragrance'), cognate with Greek ὄζω (ózō, 'to smell').

ok.etymology: Twentieth-century international borrowing from American English O.K. / okay, used in spoken Italian as an informal check or agreement.

olio.etymology: Continues Latin ŏlĕum ('olive oil'), an ancient Mediterranean word borrowed alongside Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).

oliva.etymology: Continues Latin ŏlīva ('olive fruit; olive tree'), early borrowing from archaic Greek *ἐλαίϝα (*elaíwa).

ombra.etymology: Continues Latin ŭmbra ('shadow, shade'), with regular Tuscan opening of tonic short ŭ to closed /o/.

ordinare.etymology: Continues Latin ōrdĭnāre ('to set in rows, arrange, command'), built on ōrdō, ōrdĭnis ('row, order').

ordine.etymology: Continues Latin ōrdinem (accusative of ōrdō, 'row, arrangement, command'), originally a weaving term for threads in a loom.

orecchio.etymology: Continues Latin aurĭcŭla (diminutive of auris, 'ear') via masculine reshaping *aurĭcŭlum, with au- > o- and -cl- > -cchi-.

orologiaio.etymology: Derived with agent suffix -aio (< Latin -ārius) from orologio ('clock, watch', < Latin hōrolŏgĭum < Greek ὡρολόγιον, 'hour-teller').

orologio.etymology: Continues Latin hōrologium (from Ancient Greek hōrológion, 'hour-teller', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell').

ospite.etymology: Continues Latin hospitem (accusative of hospes), which already denoted both partners of hospitality—the host who welcomes and the guest who is welcomed.

ottava.etymology: Feminine substantivisation of ottavo (< Latin octāvus, 'eighth', from ŏctō, 'eight'), short for ottava corda or ottava nota.

pagnotta.etymology: Formed on pane ('bread', < Latin pānis) with diminutive/round-shape suffix -otta (*paniotta), denoting a single round loaf.

palazzo.etymology: From Latin Palātium (the Palatine Hill in Rome, site of the imperial residences), broadening in Italian cities to mean any multi-storey masonry town building.

pane.etymology: Continues Latin pānem (accusative of pānis, 'bread'), shared with compagno ('companion', literally one who shares bread).

parlare.etymology: Continues Christian Late Latin parabolāre ('to speak in parables, converse', from Greek parabolḗ), which became the everyday word for speaking in Italian and French.

pasta.etymology: Continues Late Latin pasta ('kneaded dough, paste'), from Greek πάστη (pástē, 'barley porridge, salted meal').

pennello.etymology: Continues Latin pēnicĭllus ('small tail; painter's tuft brush'), double diminutive of pēnis ('tail').

perno.etymology: Continues Latin pĕrna ('ham, leg, wooden tenon or pivot shaped like a haunch') via Vulgar Latin *pĕrnum.

pianoforte.etymology: Shortened from gravicembalo col piano e col forte ('harpsichord with soft and loud'), coined in Florence by Bartolomeo Cristofori around 1700 for his hammer-action keyboard instrument.

piazza.etymology: Continues Latin platĕa ('broad street, open courtyard'), borrowed from Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa, 'wide way'), with regular Italian development of -tj- > -zz- and pl- > pi-.

piede.etymology: Continues Latin pēs, pĕdem ('foot'), with regular Tuscan diphthongisation of stressed open ĕ in an open syllable (pĕde > piede).

pioggia.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *ploia for classical pluvia ('rain', from pluere, 'to rain'), with pl- > pi- and -vj- > -ddʒ-.

piolo.etymology: Tuscan derivative (via *pediŏlum) of Latin pĕdĭcŭlus / pēs ('little foot, support peg, rung').

pomodoro.etymology: 16th-century compound of pomo d'oro ('golden apple'), naming the first yellow-fruited varieties brought from the Americas to Renaissance Italy.

ponte.etymology: Continues Latin pontem (accusative of pōns, 'bridge'), keeping masculine gender in Italian (il ponte).

porcellana.etymology: Originally the Old Italian name of the glossy cowrie shell (porcellana, from porcella, 'little sow'), extended by Marco Polo to translucent Chinese ceramic whose glaze resembled the shell.

porta.etymology: Continues Latin porta ('city gate, doorway'), from the Indo-European root *per- ('to pass through'), cognate with porto ('harbour') and English port.

potere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *potēre, regularized from classical posse ('to be able', contraction of potis esse).

prego.etymology: First-person singular of pregare ('to pray, ask earnestly'), from Latin precārī; shortened from vi/La prego ('I beg you / please do') into Italian's all-purpose courteous reply.

primavera.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *prīma vēra, from Classical Latin prīmō vēre ('at the start of spring', from prīmus 'first' and vēr 'spring').

qui.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(ec)cu(m) hīc ('behold here'), parallel to qua from *(ec)cu(m) hāc.

ramo.etymology: Continues Latin rāmus ('tree branch, bough'), from the accusative rāmum.

ritmo.etymology: Continues Latin rhythmus, from Greek ῥυθμός (rhythmós, 'measured flow, cadence, proportion'), related to ῥέω ('to flow').

rotolo.etymology: Continues Late Latin rŏtŭlus ('little wheel, scroll, roll'), diminutive of Latin rŏta ('wheel').

sabato.etymology: Continues Christian Latin sabbătum, borrowed via Greek σάββατον (sábbaton) from Hebrew šabbāth ('day of rest', from šābath, 'to cease from work').

sale.etymology: Continues Latin sāl, sălem ('salt'), pan-Indo-European root *séh₂ls shared with English salt and German Salz.

scaffale.etymology: Probably derived from Medieval Latin *scapha / Lombardic *skafa ('wooden tub, shelf, board'), originally designating an open set of wooden shelves for books or wares.

scala.etymology: Continues Latin scāla ('ladder, flight of steps'), related to scandere ('to climb'); used in Italian for stairs, ladders, and musical scales.

scusare.etymology: Continues Latin excūsāre ('to release from a charge, excuse', from ex- + causa), losing unstressed initial ex- > s-.

secchio.etymology: Masculine back-formation beside secchia, continuing Late Latin sĭtŭla ('water bucket, well pail') via syncopated Vulgar Latin *sĭcla.

sedia.etymology: Derived within Italian from sedere ('to sit', < Latin sedēre), naming a backed chair.

sera.etymology: From Latin sēra (diēs), feminine of sērus ('late'), naming the late hours of the day as daylight fades.

settimana.etymology: Continues Late Latin septimāna ('period of seven days'), derived from septem ('seven').

sgabello.etymology: Continues Latin scabĕllum / scamĭllum ('low footstool, step bench'), diminutive related to scamnum ('bench'), with voicing of sc- > sg-.

silenzio.etymology: Learned and popular continuation of Latin silentium ('silence, stillness'), from silēre ('to be silent').

solo.etymology: The adjective continues Latin sōlus ('alone, single'), while the adverbial sense 'only, just' continues Latin sōlum.

specchio.etymology: Continues Latin speculum ('mirror', from specere, 'to look at'), with syncope of unstressed u (speclu) and regular -cl- > -kkj-.

spendere.etymology: Continues Latin expendĕre ('to weigh out money, pay out'), with apheresis of initial ex-, from pendĕre ('to weigh').

spugna.etymology: Continues Latin spŏngĭa ('sea sponge'), borrowed from Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), with regular Tuscan palatalisation of -ngj- to /ɲɲ/.

stagista.etymology: Formed in modern Italian from French stage ('training placement', ultimately related to Old French estage, 'dwelling, period of residence') plus the agentive suffix -ista.

stare.etymology: Continues Latin stāre ('to stand, remain firm'), expanding in Italian to cover staying in a place, health/well-being (come stai?), and progressive constructions with the gerund.

stazione.etymology: From Latin statiōnem ('standing place, post, stopping point', from stāre), extended in the railway age to train and bus stations.

stoffa.etymology: Early Romance noun linked to Old French estoffe and Middle High German stouf / Old High German stopfōn ('to stuff, pad, equip with cloth').

tallone.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tālō, *tālōnem, augmentative of Classical Latin tālus ('anklebone, heel').

tavolo.etymology: Masculine back-formation from feminine tavola (< Latin tabula, 'plank, board, table'), distinguishing a piece of furniture (il tavolo) from the laid dining table (a tavola).

tempesta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tempĕsta (for Classical tempĕstās, tempestātis, 'season, weather, storm'), derived from tĕmpus ('time, weather').

tempo.etymology: Continues Latin tempus ('time, season, weather condition'), which is why one Italian word naturally covers both clock time and the weather.

terracotta.etymology: Compound of terra ('earth, clay', Latin tĕrra) + cotta ('baked, fired', feminine past participle of cuocere < Latin cŏquĕre).

tiglio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *tilius for classical feminine tilia ('linden or lime tree'), prized across Italian courtyards and avenues (viali dei tigli) for its honey-scented June blossoms.

titolo.etymology: Continues Latin tĭtŭlus ('inscription, label, heading of a scroll or book').

torta.etymology: From Late Latin tōrta (panis), originally a round 'twisted' or rolled loaf/pastry (related to torquēre, 'to twist').

treno.etymology: In its railway sense, adapted in the nineteenth century from French train and English train (ultimately from Old French traïner, 'to draw, pull along').

tu.etymology: Continues Latin tū, the inherited Indo-European singular second-person subject pronoun.

tè.etymology: Borrowed via Dutch/French thé from Hokkien (Min Nan) Chinese tê, reflecting maritime trade from Xiamen/Fujian.

uovo.etymology: Continues Latin ovum ('egg'), preserving the Latin neuter plural ending -a in its feminine Italian plural le uova.

valigia.etymology: Attested in medieval Italian (valigia) and borrowed into French as valise; of debated Late Latin or Arabic origin, naming a rider's or traveller's bag.

valzer.etymology: 19th-century loanword from German Walzer ('waltz'), agent noun from walzen ('to revolve, glide in circles').

vaso.etymology: Continues Latin vāsum (collateral masculine form of neuter vās, 'vessel, container, pot').

vassoio.etymology: Continues Late Latin missōrĭum / *vassōrĭum (crossed with vas, 'vessel, dish'), originally a flat wooden winnowing or serving tray.

vedere.etymology: Continues Latin vidēre ('to see'), with regular lowering of short Latin i to closed e in vedere.

venerdì.etymology: Continues Latin Veneris diēs ('day of Venus'), preserving the ancient planetary week in everyday speech.

venire.etymology: Continues Latin venīre ('to come'), preserving palatalized velar forms like vengo (< veniō) alongside diphthongized viene (< venit).

veramente.etymology: Formed within Italian from the feminine adjective vera ('true', from Latin vēra) plus the adverbial suffix -mente (originally Latin ablative mente, 'with a ... mind').

via.etymology: Continues Latin via ('road, way, street') unchanged in spelling; also used adverbially ('away, off') from phrases like andare per via.

volere.etymology: Continues reconstructed Vulgar Latin *volēre, regularized from classical Latin velle ('to wish, want') on analogy with present forms like volō.

zia.etymology: Continues Late Latin thĭa ('aunt'), borrowed from Byzantine Greek θεία (theía, feminine of θεῖος, 'uncle').

zucchero.etymology: Borrowed in medieval maritime Italy from Arabic sukkar ('sugar'), ultimately from Sanskrit śarkarā ('gravel, grit, crystal sugar').
